kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.claim: Roughly 21 chapters of Isaiah appear in the Book of Mormon. The wording is overwhelmingly identical to the King James Version of 1611 and 1769. That sits badly with the claim that the text was translated independently from sixth-century BC plates written in 'reformed Egyptian.' Royal Skousen's own critical-text work confirms the quotations match the standard later King James printings — not even the 1611 original. That points to a printed English Bible of Joseph Smith's own day rather than a fresh rendering of a Hebrew source. Where the Book of Mormon does vary from the King James, the variants rarely reflect a superior Hebrew reading.
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.response: FAIR and Skousen argue the translation was never a word-for-word rendering of the plates. Where the underlying record paralleled the biblical text, the familiar King James wording was given. That happened either because Joseph consulted a Bible, or — in Skousen's tight-control model — because revelation supplied King James style English. On that view the King James wording is a feature of the translation, not evidence against an ancient source. Skousen further argues that some Book of Mormon Isaiah variants reflect Early Modern English textual streams rather than copying.
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.rationale: The core datum is conceded by the leading Latter-day Saint textual scholar. The English text derives from the King James Bible, including its post-1611 printing conventions. Skousen does not dispute that. The apologetic replies reinterpret the dependence rather than rebut it.

kjv-translation-errors-copied.claim: The Book of Mormon reproduces specific King James translation errors that a rendering from an independent Hebrew source would not contain. At 2 Nephi 14:5 it has 'and upon all the glory shall be a defence,' where the Hebrew chuppah means 'canopy.' At 2 Nephi 21:3 it has 'make him of quick understanding,' misrendering a Hebrew line that says his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. At 2 Nephi 16:2 it keeps the King James double plurals 'seraphims' and 'cherubims.' These are artifacts of the 1611 translators' English, not of any ancient text. Mosiah 14 shows the same pattern.
kjv-translation-errors-copied.response: FAIR argues that a 'functional' translation aimed at a King James reading audience may keep familiar phrasing even where it is imperfect. Some of the alleged errors are defensible renderings of ambiguous Hebrew. And D&C 1:24 has God speaking to people 'after the manner of their language.' On that account the errors belong to the English translation layer rather than to the plates.
kjv-translation-errors-copied.rationale: The presence of King James specific translation artifacts is conceded. The defense relocates them to a divine translation convention. It does not show that the readings are anything other than King James errors. And no variant anywhere systematically corrects the King James back toward the Hebrew.

sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.claim: 3 Nephi 12-14 reproduces Matthew 5-7 in nearly verbatim King James English. Stan Larson identified eight passages where 3 Nephi follows readings of the late Greek manuscripts behind the King James — readings text-critical scholarship judges secondary. The clearest is the doxology at 3 Nephi 13:13, 'For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever,' which is absent from the earliest witnesses to Matthew 6:13. 'Openly' at 3 Nephi 13:4, 6 and 18 is the same kind of case. A genuine independent record of Jesus' New World sermon should not track scribal accretions of the fourth to sixteenth centuries.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.response: John W. Welch of BYU responded at length. Several of Larson's eight variants are text-critically uncertain rather than settled. One runs the other way: 3 Nephi 12:22 omits 'without a cause,' agreeing with the earliest manuscripts against the King James of Matthew 5:22. Welch also argues that the King James wording elsewhere reflects the translation register rather than the Nephite record, and that 3 Nephi's deliberate contextual adaptations show it is not mechanical copying.
sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.rationale: Welch's rebuttal engages the variants substantively, and the 'without a cause' omission is a genuine counter-datum. The doxology and 'openly' readings are still best explained by King James dependence. Scholars genuinely dispute the individual cases. The overall dependence on the King James register is not in doubt.

nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.claim: Books set between 600 and 100 BC are saturated with distinctive King James New Testament phrasing. Nephi echoes Paul — 'O wretched man that I am' at 2 Nephi 4:17 is Romans 7:24, and 'to be carnally-minded is death' at 2 Nephi 9:39 is Romans 8:6. 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes Peter's Acts 3:22-23 paraphrase of Deuteronomy 18. Alma 5:52 echoes John the Baptist at Matthew 3:10. Moroni 7:45-47 tracks 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 and Moroni 10:8-17 tracks 1 Corinthians 12:4-11, nearly verbatim. The BYU professor Nicholas Frederick has catalogued roughly 650 New Testament phrases woven through the text — language that did not exist before the first-century Greek documents it comes from.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.response: FAIR and Frederick argue the New Testament language belongs to the translation rather than the plates. Joseph Smith — or a revealed translation aimed at 1820s Bible readers — expressed Nephite concepts in the scriptural idiom his audience knew. The King James New Testament itself renders ideas with shared covenant vocabulary. Some parallels may also reflect common Old World sources, or genuinely parallel revelation of the same gospel to prophets before Christ.
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.rationale: The datum is conceded even at BYU. Hundreds of distinctively New Testament phrases pervade the text. The translation-idiom defense does not rebut the dependence. It concedes that the English text is not a literal rendering of an ancient record. And it strains hardest where New Testament passages structure whole sermons.

hebrews-in-alma-12-13.claim: David Wright showed that Alma's sermon, dated to about 82 BC, reproduces the Epistle to the Hebrews. Alma 12:9-37 and 13:1-20 follow the distinctive argument sequence, exegetical moves and King James wording of Hebrews 3:7-4:11 and 7:1-4 — priesthood 'after the order of the Son,' Melchizedek, and entering God's 'rest.' Alma 13:17-19's Melchizedek summary tracks Hebrews 7:1-4 closely. Scholars regard those elements as the author of Hebrews' own creative synthesis of Genesis 14 and Psalm 110, which no pre-Christian source contained.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13.response: John W. Welch and the FARMS reviewers argued that Alma 13 and Hebrews could draw independently on older Melchizedek traditions. Such traditions are attested in Second Temple texts, including 11QMelchizedek and the Genesis Apocryphon. The shared King James wording is translation register. And Alma's treatment diverges from Hebrews in emphasis — repentance and ordination rather than Christ's superiority — which straightforward dependence would not predict.
hebrews-in-alma-12-13.rationale: Wright's verbal and structural case is detailed and has not been dismantled. The common-tradition hypothesis is a substantive alternative, though no manuscript supports it directly, and it does not simply concede dependence. The dispute is genuine. The parallels favor Wright.

mark-long-ending-mormon-9.claim: Mormon 9:22-24 has the resurrected Jesus commissioning the Nephite disciples in words nearly identical to Mark 16:15-18 in the King James. Ether 4:18 draws on the same material. That is the 'long ending' of Mark, which is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Mainstream textual criticism judges it a second-century scribal addition. The Book of Mormon therefore attributes to Jesus in America a saying that, on the scholarly consensus, entered Mark's text after the first century.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9.response: Book of Mormon Central, in KnoWhy 522, gives two replies. A minority of credentialed non-Latter-day-Saint scholars — Nicholas Lunn and James Snapp — defend the long ending's authenticity on patristic and internal grounds. Alternatively, even if Mark 16:9-20 is secondary, Moroni's source was the Nephite record of Christ's words, and the King James phrasing is translation register. The resurrected Lord could have given the same commission in both hemispheres.
mark-long-ending-mormon-9.rationale: The apologetic depends on a minority text-critical position. That position does have genuine published non-Latter-day-Saint defenders, so the underlying question of the long ending's authenticity is disputed. Under the majority view the criticism stands unanswered.

horses-anachronism.claim: The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes horses among Jaredites and Nephites, from about 2500 BC to AD 400, including horses harnessed to 'chariots' — 1 Nephi 18:25, Enos 1:21, Alma 18:9-12, 3 Nephi 3:22 and Ether 9:19. Equids went extinct in the Americas around 10,000 BC and were reintroduced by the Spanish in the sixteenth century. Despite extensive archaeological and paleontological sampling, no verified pre-Columbian Holocene horse remains, depictions or loanwords exist. The related Old World animals the text names — cattle, oxen, asses, swine and the elephants of Ether 9:19 — face the same null record.
horses-anachronism.response: Book of Mormon Central and FAIR offer three lines. 'Horse' may be a loanshift, the translation applying a familiar label to a native animal such as a deer or a tapir, exactly as Spaniards and native peoples did with unfamiliar fauna. Small relict horse populations may have survived into Book of Mormon times undetected; Wade Miller has had candidate late-dated remains tested. And absence of evidence carries little weight in tropical conditions, where bone rarely survives.
horses-anachronism.rationale: No verified pre-Columbian Holocene horse has been produced. Radiocarbon tests of candidate remains come back either Pleistocene or post-contact. The loanshift defense concedes the core point, that no actual horses were present. And the text's horses-with-chariots imagery resists the tapir substitution. Michael Coe of Yale set the problem out in Dialogue in 1973.

steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.claim: The Book of Mormon describes New World steel and iron working. Nephi carries a 'bow of steel' from Arabia. Nephites teach the making of 'steel' and working 'in all manner of iron,' around 590 to 400 BC. Jaredites have steel swords at Ether 7:9. Archaeology finds no ferrous metallurgy anywhere in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica — no smelting sites, no slag, no tools, no iron or steel weapons. Metallurgy of any kind appears in Mesoamerica only around AD 600 to 800, and it never included iron smelting.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.response: On the Old World references the defense is strong. The Vered Jericho carburized-steel sword, dated about 620 BC and held in the Israel Museum, shows that 'most precious steel' was real in Lehi's Jerusalem. That is a genuine vindication. For the New World, FAIR makes three points. 'Steel' in King James English can mean any hardened metal; the King James uses it to render Hebrew bronze. Mesoamericans did work meteoric iron. And a limited-scale Nephite metallurgy could have left little trace, with its terminology a loanshift.
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.rationale: The Old World steel references are genuinely answered by the Vered Jericho sword. The distinct core claim is not: a Nephite and Jaredite iron-and-steel industry in the Americas has zero archaeological support. Michael Coe and Deanne Matheny have both pressed this. The semantic loanshift defense concedes that no actual steel existed, while the text describes people being taught to manufacture it.

wheat-barley-silk.claim: The Book of Mormon describes Nephites and Jaredites cultivating wheat and barley and producing silk — Mosiah 9:9, Alma 1:29, Ether 9:17 and Ether 10:24. Old World wheat (Triticum), barley (Hordeum vulgare) and silkworm sericulture are absent from the pre-Columbian archaeological and botanical record. New World agriculture centred on maize, beans and squash. Barley is also embedded in the text's Mosaic-law economy at Alma 11:7 and 11:15 — a system of weights, not coins. The 'coins' chapter heading was a twentieth-century editorial addition, since corrected.
wheat-barley-silk.response: Apologists note that domesticated little barley (Hordeum pusillum), unknown to scholarship in 1830, has since been confirmed as a cultivated pre-Columbian North American grain. On that ground 'barley' is no longer a clean anachronism. 'Wheat' and 'silk' are defended as loanshifts — a familiar label for comparable native grains such as amaranth, and for fine indigenous fibres such as kapok and the wild-silk textiles attested in Mesoamerica.
wheat-barley-silk.rationale: The little-barley find gives the apologetic case real traction on barley, even though the species has shifted, and wild-silk textiles are genuinely attested. Old World wheat remains wholly unattested. The loanshift defense again concedes that the named referents were absent. The dispute is genuine but asymmetric. Michael Coe set out the original problem in Dialogue in 1973.

greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.claim: The Book of Mormon has Greek names in a Hebrew colony. Timothy and Jonas appear at 3 Nephi 19:4. Lachoneus appears at 3 Nephi 1:1; the name means 'the Laconian.' At 3 Nephi 9:18 the risen Jesus calls himself 'Alpha and Omega.' Those are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. The phrase is drawn from Revelation 1:8. But Lehi's people left Jerusalem in 600 BC and wrote in 'reformed Egyptian.' They had no Greek contact.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.response: Hugh Nibley and Stephen Ricks argue that Greeks were in Lehi's world. From the mid-600s BC, Ionian and Carian soldiers and traders served Egypt. They fought in the army of Necho II and worked across the Levant. So a Greek name could reach Lehi's people, or more easily the Mulekites. There is a second line too. 'Timothy,' 'Jonas' and 'Alpha and Omega' may be the translator's English stand-ins for Nephite names and sayings.
greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.rationale: The mercenary reply rests on real history. Greeks were in Egypt and the Levant in the 600s BC. And the stand-in reading works well for 'Alpha and Omega.' Two things still fit an 1829 writer better. One is 'Lachoneus' as a personal name. The other is wording that matches Revelation exactly. Grant Palmer made that case. Neither side has a decisive case.

church-bible-synagogue-terms.claim: The text uses institutional terms that postdate its setting. 'Church' describes Jerusalem in 600 BC at 1 Nephi 4:26, and formal Nephite institutions before Christ. 'Synagogues' appear at 2 Nephi 26:26, Alma 16:13 and Alma 21:4-6, before the institution developed after the exile. And Nephi uses the word 'Bible' at 2 Nephi 29:3-10 — a term from the Greek biblia, first applied to the scriptural codex centuries after Christ. That passage anticipates and rebuts a nineteenth-century objection: 'A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible.'
church-bible-synagogue-terms.response: FAIR responds that 'church' and 'synagogue' are the English translator's institutional vocabulary for whatever assemblies the Nephites had, and that King James usage of 'church' is similarly elastic. The synagogue scholar Lee Levine and others allow for pre-exilic communal worship settings, such as gate chambers. And 'Bible' occurs inside an explicit prophecy of the latter days, where foreknowledge of the future artifact is precisely the point.
church-bible-synagogue-terms.rationale: As pure vocabulary, 'church' and 'synagogue' are adequately handled by any translation theory, since translators routinely use target-language institutional terms. That defense sits awkwardly with Skousen's tight-control evidence. And the 2 Nephi 29 'Bible' passage, functioning as a rebuttal to nineteenth-century critics, remains better evidence of nineteenth-century composition than of prophecy.

dark-skin-curse.claim: The Book of Mormon teaches that God cursed the Lamanites with 'a skin of blackness' so they would not be enticing to the righteous Nephites (2 Nephi 5:21-23). Alma 3:6-9 marks their descendants the same way, and 3 Nephi 2:14-15 describes converted Lamanites' skin becoming white. Jacob 3:8-9 and Mormon 5:15 belong with these. That contradicts the biblical teaching that God made all nations of one blood (Acts 17:26). It contradicts Acts 10:34-35, where he shows no partiality, and 1 Samuel 16:7, where he looks on the heart rather than the outward appearance. Galatians 3:28, John 7:24 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way. The church's own edits are cited as tacit admission that the racial reading is the natural one. In 1981, 'white and delightsome' became 'pure and delightsome' at 2 Nephi 30:6. In 2010, racial language was removed from the chapter headings of 2 Nephi 5 and Mormon 5.
dark-skin-curse.response: Scripture Central and recent BYU scholarship, including Ethan Sproat and Gerrit Steenblik, argue that 'skin of blackness' may be metaphorical, or may refer to garments and marks the Lamanites adopted, rather than to pigmentation. On that reading the curse itself was separation from the Lord at 2 Nephi 5:20, with the 'mark' a distinct thing. FAIR notes that the text itself condemns Nephite racism, since Jacob 3:5-9 says the Lamanites were more righteous. FAIR adds that some episodes have the two peoples indistinguishable, which makes little sense if the skin difference were literal and stark. The heading edits corrected uninspired 1981 study helps written by Bruce R. McConkie, not the revealed text. The 2013 Gospel Topics essay 'Race and the Priesthood' disavows the theory that dark skin signals divine disfavour.
dark-skin-curse.rationale: The metaphorical and garment reading is a late apologetic development. It contradicts nearly two centuries of the church's own authoritative interpretation, from Brigham Young through Spencer W. Kimball, who reported Lamanite converts becoming lighter. The text's causal chain resists it: cursed 'because of their iniquity,' therefore 'a skin of blackness,' 'that they might not be enticing.' 3 Nephi 2:15 has the curse and the skin change together. The 2013 disavowal effectively concedes the criticism against the text's plain sense rather than refuting it.

fortunate-fall.claim: 2 Nephi 2:22-25 teaches that Adam's fall was necessary and good. Without it Adam and Eve 'would have had no children,' and 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.' Alma 12:22-26 follows the same line. Critics argue this contradicts the Bible, which presents the fall as sin bringing death and condemnation (Romans 5:12-19, Romans 8:20-22), never as the enabling condition of procreation. God commanded 'be fruitful, and multiply' at Genesis 1:28, before the fall. That makes the Book of Mormon's premise a direct contradiction, and makes God the author of a transgression he forbade in the same breath. 1 Timothy 2:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 point the same way.
fortunate-fall.response: The BYU Religious Studies Center, in 'The Fortunate Fall of Adam and Eve,' situates the doctrine inside the venerable Christian felix culpa tradition. Ambrose taught it, Augustine wrote 'O felix culpa,' and the Easter Exsultet sings it. On that tradition the fall occasions a greater good, the Incarnation, so a providential fall is not foreign to Christianity. Scripture Central adds that Lehi's point is structural: mortality, agency and the capacity for joy require a world built on opposition, as 2 Nephi 2:11 says. The fall was a 'transgression' of a lesser law rather than sin in the fullest sense — a distinction some Christian theologians also draw. And Eve is honoured rather than blamed, which Latter-day Saints present as a strength.
fortunate-fall.rationale: The felix culpa parallel is a genuine steelman. Christianity has long held that God brings a greater good out of the fall. It does not reach the specific claims here. 2 Nephi 2 says the fall was required for procreation, which runs flatly against the pre-fall command of Genesis 1:28. It also says Adam and Eve 'would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy.' The felix culpa tradition celebrates redemption despite the fall. 2 Nephi 2 makes the fall itself instrumentally necessary. That is a materially different claim, and the Genesis 1:28 point still has no strong published answer.

original-sin-infant-baptism.claim: Moroni 8 declares that little children 'are not capable of committing sin.' It calls infant baptism 'solemn mockery before God.' And it says that anyone who supposes children need baptism 'must go down to hell' if he dies in that thought (Moroni 8:8-23). Mosiah 3:16-21 and 2 Nephi 2:25 support it. Critics set this against the Bible. Psalm 51:5 says we are sinful from conception. Ephesians 2:3 calls us 'by nature the children of wrath.' Romans 5:12 and 18-19 say we are condemned in Adam, and so do Genesis 8:21, Psalm 58:3 and 1 Corinthians 15:22. Critics add two points. The position mirrors the Pelagian controversy settled in AD 418. And damning most of historic Christendom, which practised infant baptism, goes far past any biblical warrant.
original-sin-infant-baptism.response: FAIR makes three points. First, the Bible never commands infant baptism and never shows one. Baptists and most evangelicals agree with the Book of Mormon's practical conclusion. So this is not a simple Bible versus Book of Mormon conflict. It tracks a dispute among Christians. Second, original sin as inherited guilt is an Augustinian development. Eastern Orthodoxy rejects inherited guilt and keeps only inherited corruption and mortality. Psalm 51:5 is Davidic poetry about how deep sin runs, not a dogma of infant guilt. Third, Latter-day Saint teaching holds that Christ's atonement covers Adam's fall for children with no conditions. Moroni 8:8 says 'the curse of Adam is taken from them in me.' So children are redeemed, not merely innocent.
original-sin-infant-baptism.rationale: As a proof-text battle the critics overreach. Infant baptism is disputed among Bible-affirming Christians. So is inherited guilt. The Latter-day Saint reply correctly finds allies for parts of its position. What survives is narrower but real. Moroni 8 sends infant-baptizers to hell. That condemns nearly all pre-Reformation Christianity, with a severity no biblical text licenses. And the passage argues a post-biblical fight inside a text presented as fourth-century American. The fight is Pelagius against Augustine, plus nineteenth-century revivalism. That shades into a problem about where the text came from.

no-semitic-inscriptions.claim: The Book of Mormon describes a thousand years of continuous record-keeping. Scribes write Hebrew and a modified Egyptian script on metal plates and stone — Mormon 9:32-34, 1 Nephi 1:2, Omni 1:20-22, Mosiah 8:11-13, Jacob 4:1-3. No pre-Columbian inscription in Hebrew, Egyptian or any Semitic-derived script has ever been authenticated in the Americas. No script called 'reformed Egyptian' is attested in Egyptology. The writing systems we can read there are Maya, Zapotec and Epi-Olmec. None is related to Afro-Asiatic writing in structure or in sign inventory. Four objects are periodically advanced as exceptions. They are the Bat Creek Stone, the Los Lunas Decalogue Stone, the Newark Holy Stones and the Michigan Relics. All four are documented or strongly suspected forgeries.
no-semitic-inscriptions.response: Three replies. First, 'reformed Egyptian' is the text's own phrase for its script, 'altered by us, according to our manner of speech,' at Mormon 9:32. It is not a claim that Egyptologists should recognise the name. Egyptian really was reformed over time, from hieroglyphic to hieratic to demotic. Hugh Nibley noted documented cases of Semitic languages written in Egyptian characters. Second, the record was a small elite tradition on metal plates. A few men kept it, and then it was buried. It was never a habit of public monuments, so we would not expect to find it. Third, Brian Stubbs, a specialist in Uto-Aztecan, argues for about 1,500 proposed Semitic and Egyptian matches in Uto-Aztecan. He claims regular sound correspondences, which is the kind of evidence historical linguistics accepts.
no-semitic-inscriptions.rationale: The small-corpus argument is internally coherent. It also concedes that the claim cannot be tested. Stubbs's work is the only substantive positive evidence. No historical linguist outside the church has accepted it or engaged it seriously. The standard criticism is that his method searches a large word list for sound resemblances. Given enough candidates, it can turn up similar matches between unrelated language families. Meanwhile the null result stands. A whole field of decipherment has found no Afro-Asiatic link in any Mesoamerican script, as Michael Coe of Yale has said.

dna-native-american-origins.claim: Mitochondrial, Y-chromosome and autosomal studies place essentially all pre-Columbian Native American ancestry in Siberian and East Asian source populations entering via Beringia more than 15,000 years ago. No Middle Eastern founding lineage from about 600 BC has been identified. Two Latter-day Saint scientists published this as a direct falsification of the Lamanite claim in 2002 and 2003 — Thomas Murphy, an anthropologist, and Simon Southerton, a geneticist and former bishop. Murphy faced a disciplinary council, postponed 24 hours before it convened, and Southerton was disciplined. In 2006 the church silently changed the Book of Mormon introduction: the Lamanites went from 'the principal ancestors of the American Indians' to 'among the ancestors.' The Title Page, 1 Nephi 13:30, 2 Nephi 30:4-6, Alma 10:3, Helaman 15:11-13 and 3 Nephi 21:2-7 are the texts at issue.
dna-native-american-origins.response: The church's own Gospel Topics essay concedes that 'the majority of Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA,' then answers on five fronts. Nothing in the text claims Lehi's party was the only population; the introduction was a 1981 editorial addition rather than scripture, and 2006 corrected an over-reading. A founding party of about 30 entering an already-large population would leave a signal below detection after 2,600 years, which is standard population genetics rather than special pleading. Founder effect, genetic drift and the post-contact bottleneck each erase small founding lineages, and we do not know the ancient Israelite genetic profile to look for. Ugo Perego, a population geneticist, notes that the Asian ancestor of haplogroup X2a is itself undetected in modern Asia — proof that real founding lineages go missing. The essay's own bottom line is that DNA studies 'cannot be used decisively to either affirm or reject' the Book of Mormon.
dna-native-american-origins.rationale: The population-genetics rebuttal is technically sound. Drift, founder effects and the bottleneck genuinely can erase a small founding lineage, and critics who claim DNA 'disproves' the book overstate what a null result can do. The concession is nonetheless enormous. The defense works only by shrinking the Book of Mormon peoples into a demographically marginal group inside a continent already full of Asians. That contradicts the text's self-presentation — 2 Nephi 1:8-9 has the land 'kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations' — and 150 years of prophetic teaching. And it required an unannounced edit to the printed introduction, the most concrete institutional concession in this entire list.

population-growth-impossible.claim: A founding party of roughly 20 to 30 people arrives about 589 BC. It splits almost at once into Nephites and Lamanites. Within about 500 years the text reports 19,094 Lamanites slain in a single battle (Alma 2:19). Armies of tens of thousands appear throughout Alma, and 230,000 Nephites are killed at Cumorah (Mormon 6:10-15). The Jaredites reach 'two millions' (Ether 15:2). John Kunich showed that reaching these figures from the stated founders needs sustained growth rates far above anything seen in pre-modern populations. The text also has the Nephites building temples, and fielding kings and standing armies, within two generations of a landing party of a couple of dozen — 1 Nephi 18:23, 2 Nephi 5:6-16, Jarom 1:8, Alma 28:2.
population-growth-impossible.response: James E. Smith is a professional historical demographer. Writing in FARMS Review 6/1 in 1994, he argues that Kunich misapplies long-run averages to a colonizing group. Frontier populations with land to spare routinely sustain 2 to 3% a year for centuries. Colonial New England and Pitcairn are examples. Smith's model-life-table runs produce Book of Mormon numbers under defensible assumptions. Polygamy is attested among Lamanites and early Nephites too. The strongest point is textual, not ad hoc. The book never says the land was empty. Sherem appears from nowhere in Jacob 7. The Mulekites are found already numerous in Omni 1. And 'Lamanite' works as a political label. If Lehi's party joined peoples already there, no impossible growth rate is needed. Finally, ancient casualty numbers are notoriously inflated — biblical, classical and Mesoamerican alike — so reading them as census data is a category error.
population-growth-impossible.rationale: This is the criticism the Latter-day Saint side has answered best on its own terms. Smith is a credentialed demographer. His frontier-growth objection to Kunich is technically correct, and the 'others in the land' reading is textually defensible. But the fix is costly, and it creates a squeeze. The more 'others' are imported to solve the demography and the DNA, the less the book is what its own narrators thought it was. Its nineteenth-century readers thought the same. And the text's total silence about a surrounding native majority then becomes strange in itself. On its own this does not sink the text. It works as a force multiplier on the DNA and archaeology entries.

nephite-non-levite-priesthood.claim: The Book of Mormon says the Nephites kept the law of Moses strictly (2 Nephi 5:10; 25:24) and offered burnt sacrifices (1 Nephi 5:9; Mosiah 2:3). Yet Nephi — of the tribe of Joseph through Manasseh (Alma 10:3) — consecrates his brothers Jacob and Joseph as priests (2 Nephi 5:26; Jacob 1:18). The Mosaic law restricted the priesthood and sacrificial service to Aaron's line within Levi (Numbers 3:9-12; 16:39-40; Deuteronomy 33:8-11), and Hebrews 7:13-14 states plainly that of a non-Levite tribe 'no man gave attendance at the altar.' 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 shows the penalty. Critics argue that a genuinely law-observant Israelite colony could not run a non-Levitical sacrificial priesthood while claiming to keep the law of Moses.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood.response: Apologists argue the Nephites held the higher Melchizedek priesthood. Jacob was ordained 'after the manner of his holy order' (2 Nephi 6:2), and Alma 13 develops the idea. That order biblically predates and transcends Levi — Genesis 14, Psalm 110, Hebrews 7:4-10 — so Levitical restrictions did not bind them. They add that the Book of Mormon never claims Levitical authority for these priests, that no Levites travelled with Lehi's party, and that Jewish communities of exactly Lehi's era operated sacrificial sites outside the Levitical Jerusalem system, at Elephantine and Arad. FAIR concludes the practice was not unthinkable for diaspora Israelites.
nephite-non-levite-priesthood.rationale: The Melchizedek-order reading has an internal textual basis in Alma 13, and Elephantine gives real historical precedent for irregular diaspora practice. But Hebrews 7 treats a non-Levitical priesthood as incompatible with the Mosaic law the Nephites claim to be keeping 'in all things.' The tension between strict law observance and a non-Aaronic altar remains unresolved.

temples-outside-jerusalem.claim: Nephi builds a temple 'after the manner of the temple of Solomon' (2 Nephi 5:16), and the Book of Mormon later describes temples in multiple cities (Alma 16:13; 26:29; Helaman 3:9, 14). Deuteronomy 12:5-14 confines sacrificial worship to 'the place which the LORD your God shall choose,' understood after Solomon as the Jerusalem temple alone (1 Kings 8:29). Josiah's reform, within living memory of Lehi's departure, had specifically destroyed rival sanctuaries (2 Kings 23:4-20). A colony professing strict Mosaic observance while multiplying temples runs against the law's command to worship in one place.
temples-outside-jerusalem.response: FAIR points to Jewish temples outside Jerusalem, from Lehi's own time or soon after. There was a temple with sacrifice at Elephantine in Egypt. There was a sanctuary at Arad. Leontopolis came later. So Jews far from Jerusalem did in fact build temples. FAIR argues that the one-place rule of Deuteronomy 12 applied inside the land of Israel. It did not bind a group cut off from that land across an ocean. On that reading Nephi's temple is what a devout but permanently separated colony would do.
temples-outside-jerusalem.rationale: Elephantine and Arad are real sites, dug up and dated. They blunt the claim that this was unthinkable. But scholars judge those altars irregular against the law of Deuteronomy. The Book of Mormon presents Nephite temples as fully proper. So the clash with Deuteronomy 12 stands as a matter of law, even though the practice has precedent in history.

christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.claim: The Book of Mormon's centerpiece is the resurrected Christ descending to minister bodily to the Nephites for days (3 Nephi 11:8-17; 26:13). Critics set this against Peter's statement that Jesus is one 'whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things' (Acts 3:20-21; cf. Acts 1:9-11). The argument is that the New Testament expects Christ to remain in heaven between the ascension and the last days, leaving no room for an extended post-ascension earthly ministry in the Americas.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.response: Apologists reply that the New Testament itself records post-ascension appearances of Christ — to Stephen (Acts 7:55-56), to Paul on the Damascus road (Acts 9:3-6; 1 Corinthians 15:8), and to John on Patmos (Revelation 1:12-18). So Acts 3:21 cannot mean Christ never appears before the restitution. It describes his heavenly residence, not a prohibition on visitation. The Nephite ministry is claimed to be the same kind of appearance at larger scale, and 'other sheep I have' (John 10:16) is read as Jesus's own anticipation of it.
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.rationale: The strong reading of Acts 3:21 — no earthly appearance until the end — is defeated by the New Testament's own post-ascension appearances to Stephen, Paul and John. Whatever other problems 3 Nephi has, and they are covered elsewhere, this particular verse does not textually exclude an appearance. Christians should drop it.

joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.claim: D&C 84:2-5, given in September 1832, declares that a temple 'shall be reared in this generation' on the dedicated lot in Independence, Missouri — 'verily this generation shall not all pass away until an house shall be built unto the Lord.' No temple was ever built there, and every member of that generation is long dead. Critics apply Deuteronomy 18:20-22: a prophet whose predicted thing 'follow not, nor come to pass' has spoken presumptuously. Jeremiah 28:9 and Ezekiel 33:33 are used the same way. Related cases include D&C 114:1, where David W. Patten is called to a mission 'next spring' though he was killed months earlier, and the 1835 statement about the Second Coming in fifty-six years.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.response: FAIR argues that biblical prophecy is often implicitly conditional on human obedience. Jonah's unqualified 'forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown' did not come to pass, and Jonah was no false prophet. D&C 124:49-51, from 1841, canonizes exactly this principle: when enemies prevent a commanded work, God 'requires that work no more.' The Saints were violently expelled from Jackson County in 1833, which made the temple impossible. Alternative readings take verse 5's 'an house' as fulfilled by the Kirtland temple in 1836, or treat the words as a directive rather than a flat prediction.
joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.rationale: The non-fulfillment is an undisputed fact, and the 'this generation shall not all pass away' formula reads as an unconditional, time-bound oracle. Later leaders such as Orson Pratt kept reaffirming it as one. Yet the Jonah precedent and the in-canon conditionality clause of D&C 124:49 give the Latter-day Saint response genuine biblical and textual footing. The argument therefore turns on contested hermeneutics rather than on settled fact.

exaltation-eternal-progression.claim: Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that the faithful sealed in celestial marriage 'shall pass by the angels, and the gods… Then shall they be gods, because they have no end… because they have all power' (D&C 132:19-20; cf. 132:37, Abraham 3:22-26). Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse of 1844 taught that God 'was once a man like us' and that the Saints must learn 'how to be gods yourselves.' Lorenzo Snow crystallized it: as man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be. The church's 2014 essay 'Becoming Like God' complains that this is reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets — yet reaffirms the substance, exaltation to godhood with divine creative capacity. Critics set this against Yahweh's own words: 'before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me' (Isaiah 43:10; cf. 44:6-8, 45:5, Psalm 90:2). They note that the first promise of godhood in Scripture came from the serpent — 'ye shall be as gods' (Genesis 3:5).
exaltation-eternal-progression.response: The essay's steelman is that deification language pervades early Christianity. Psalm 82:6, quoted by Jesus at John 10:34, says 'Ye are gods.' 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of 'partakers of the divine nature,' and Romans 8:17 of being 'joint-heirs with Christ.' Church fathers from Irenaeus to Clement of Alexandria taught it; Clement wrote that the Word of God became man 'that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God.' On that reading Latter-day Saint exaltation restores an ancient doctrine of theosis rather than inventing polytheism. Isaiah's denials are read as directed at idols and rival gods, not at God's own children inheriting his nature. Exalted beings remain eternally subordinate to the Father, and the essay stresses that little has been revealed about the couplet's first half.
exaltation-eternal-progression.rationale: The doctrinal content is established from the church's own canon and its current essay, which disavows the planet caricature while reaffirming godhood with creative capacity. The theosis steelman fails to close the gap. Patristic deification explicitly preserved the Creator-creature distinction. It never taught that God was once a man, and never taught that the deified become gods in the ontological sense D&C 132 describes. Isaiah 43:10's 'no God formed… after me' is left in direct tension.

heavenly-mother-doctrine.claim: The church's 2015 essay 'Mother in Heaven' affirms as 'cherished and distinctive' doctrine that all human spirits are children of a Heavenly Father and a Heavenly Mother. It is rooted in Joseph Smith's teaching of spirit pre-existence (Abraham 3:22-26; D&C 93:29; D&C 132:19-20) and was popularized by Eliza R. Snow's hymn 'O My Father.' The essay concedes that 'our present knowledge about a Mother in Heaven is limited,' and that 'there is no record of a formal revelation to Joseph Smith on this doctrine.' It directs that members not pray to her. Critics note that the Bible is wholly silent on a divine Mother. The only 'queen of heaven' it mentions is an idolatrous cult that Jeremiah condemns (Jeremiah 7:18; 44:17-25). And divine parents procreating spirits sits uneasily with 'the LORD is one' (Deuteronomy 6:4), 'beside me there is no God' (Isaiah 44:6-8), and John 4:24.
heavenly-mother-doctrine.response: The essay, together with David Paulsen and Martin Pulido's survey of some 600 historical references in BYU Studies, presents Heavenly Mother as a reasoned corollary of restored truths. If humans are literally God's spirit children, made 'male and female' in the divine image at Genesis 1:26-27, then eternal parenthood implies a Mother. Biblical silence is not denial, since Latter-day Saints do not hold the Bible to be doctrinally exhaustive. Worship and prayer remain directed solely to the Father in Christ's name, following Jesus's own pattern, so the doctrine is framed as honouring rather than worshipping a second divine being.
heavenly-mother-doctrine.rationale: The core factual claim is conceded in the essay itself: an affirmed doctrine resting on no biblical text and, by the church's own admission, no recorded formal revelation. The argument-from-corollary steelman is coherent within Latter-day Saint premises, but it supplies no scriptural attestation. That is the point at issue.

jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.claim: Official Latter-day Saint doctrine teaches that Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of Heavenly Father and heavenly parents — 'the firstborn of the spirit children of our Heavenly Father,' in Gospel Principles chapters 2 and 3. That makes him the literal elder brother of all humans, of the same kind as us, who progressed to divinity in the premortal world. James Talmage's Jesus the Christ says Christ 'attained the rank of Godhood' premortally. The Bible teaches that Christ is the eternal, uncreated Creator. 'All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made' (John 1:3) — a scope that excludes Christ himself from the category of things that came to be. He 'is before all things' (Colossians 1:17). His goings forth are 'from of old, from everlasting' (Micah 5:2). He is 'the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever' (Hebrews 13:8), and says 'before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58). A being begotten as one spirit child among billions, who then attains godhood, is a different kind of being from one who eternally is God.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.response: Apologists reply that Jesus did not become divine late or from nothing meaningful. He is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament — 'He was the Great Jehovah of the Old Testament,' in The Living Christ of 2000 — fully divine before creation. He created 'worlds without number' under the Father's direction (Moses 1:33), and D&C 93:21 calls him 'the Firstborn' who was 'in the beginning with the Father.' On Colossians 1:15 they note that Paul himself calls Christ 'the firstborn of every creature.' FAIR argues that the Greek in Colossians 1:16 connotes organizing existing material rather than creation from nothing, so 'all things were made by him' need not include eternally existing spirit-matter or Christ's own spirit. Firstborn status, they argue, denotes preeminence and heirship, as at Psalm 89:27 — which Latter-day Saint theology affirms maximally.
jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.rationale: The doctrine is accurately documented from current official sources, and the conflict is structural rather than a proof-text quibble. Even granting that Christ as Jehovah was divine 'before the world was,' this theology still makes him a begotten spirit sibling of humanity whose divinity was attained — one of us who rose, rather than the eternal Creator who condescended. John 1:3's exhaustive scope, and Colossians 1:17's 'he is before all things,' leave no category of self-existent spirit-stuff or sibling spirits that Christ did not create. The Latter-day Saint reading must carve out exactly the exceptions the text forecloses. And the 'firstborn of every creature' steelman fails against verse 16's own explanation, 'for by him were all things created.' The firstborn is preeminent over creation because he made it.

js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.claim: Joseph Smith was sealed to approximately 30 to 40 women. The figure is the church's own: the Gospel Topics essay says 'careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40.' Among them was Helen Mar Kimball, sealed 'several months before her 15th birthday' — that is, at 14. Another was Fanny Alger, about 16, a servant in the Smith home. Oliver Cowdery called that relationship 'a dirty, nasty, filthy scrape' in a letter of 21 January 1838. Cowdery was excommunicated shortly afterwards, charged with 'falsely insinuating' that Smith was guilty of adultery. Most of the sealings were concealed from Emma Smith and from the church at large. Jacob 2:24 and 2:27-28 stand against the practice, as do 1 Timothy 3:2 and Matthew 19:4-6.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.response: The church acknowledges the marriages. It frames them as a commanded restoration of Old Testament plural marriage, which Smith resisted — hence the accounts of an angel with a drawn sword. Brian Hales argues that Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely 'eternity only' and dynastic, linking the Kimball and Smith families, with no evidence of conjugality. Helen continued to live with her parents. Marriage at 14 to 16, while young, was legal and not unheard of on the 1840s frontier. And on late reminiscences, Fanny Alger was a marriage with parental consent rather than an affair. Cowdery's description is that of an estranged critic.
js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.rationale: The core facts are conceded in the church's own essay: 30 to 40 wives, a 14-year-old bride, and secrecy from Emma and from the church. The apologetic arguments go to interpretation — eternity-only sealings, dynastic purpose — rather than to the facts. The eternity-only reading of the Kimball sealing is possible but unprovable. And 1840s norms do not explain the concealment. The claim as stated is documented by the institution itself.

js-polyandry.claim: Joseph Smith was sealed to roughly 11 women who were civilly married to living husbands at the time. Todd Compton puts that at about a third of his plural wives. Zina Diantha Huntington was sealed to Smith in October 1841, about seven months after she married Henry Jacobs. Smith had relayed that an angel with a drawn sword threatened his position and his life if plural marriage was not established. She continued living with Jacobs. The church's own Gospel Topics essay concedes that Smith was sealed to 'a number of women who were already married.' Jacob 2:27 forbids it, and so do Romans 7:2-3, Mark 10:11-12 and Exodus 20:14.
js-polyandry.response: Brian Hales argues that most polyandrous sealings were 'eternity only' — a linkage for the next life that did not disturb the earthly marriage. That is why husbands such as Henry Jacobs remained in the home, and why some stayed faithful members. There is supporting evidence. In 2016, DNA testing by Ugo Perego excluded Smith as the father of Josephine Lyon, whose mother was the polyandrous wife with the strongest documentary claim of conjugality. No verified child of Smith by any plural wife has been identified. The essay itself states that these sealings may have been about eternal linkage rather than earthly marital relations.
js-polyandry.rationale: The fact of sealings to married women is conceded by the church. Whether they included sexual relations is genuinely contested, and the DNA evidence is a real apologetic win. Critics who assert proven sexual polyandry overreach. But the claim as stated stands on primary sources: sealings to other men's wives, under angelic threat, concealed from the community.

dc132-emma-destroyed.claim: Doctrine and Covenants 132 was dictated on 12 July 1843. It is still canonized Latter-day Saint scripture today. It addresses Emma Smith by name. Verse 52 commands her to 'receive all those that have been given unto my servant Joseph.' Verse 54 warns that 'if she will not abide this commandment she shall be destroyed, saith the Lord.' Verse 64 generalizes the threat to any first wife who refuses consent. The revelation was dictated after Smith had already married most of his plural wives, without Emma's knowledge or consent. Ephesians 5:25, 1 Peter 3:7 and Colossians 3:19 set a different standard for husbands.
dc132-emma-destroyed.response: Apologists read 'destroyed' as covenant language rather than physical death — the forfeiture of covenant blessings, paralleling verse 26. They note that no harm ever came to Emma. She refused, burned the copy of the revelation, and remained Smith's wife. The revelation is framed as an Abrahamic test, and the sections addressing Emma also promise blessings for obedience. Richard Bushman notes that it was committed to writing at Hyrum's request, specifically to persuade Emma. On that reading it reflects a domestic crisis, not a death threat.
dc132-emma-destroyed.rationale: The text and its canonical status are undisputed. Anyone can read it in the current Doctrine and Covenants. The softened reading of 'destroyed' is a plausible gloss. It does not change the fact that canonized scripture conditions a named woman's fate on accepting her husband's additional wives. The factual claim is fully documented.

js-polygamy-denials.claim: On 26 May 1844, a month before his death, Joseph Smith preached publicly: 'What a thing it is for a man to be accused of committing adultery, and having seven wives, when I can only find one.' It is recorded in History of the Church 6:411. By that date he had been sealed to more than 30 women. This capped years of institutional denials. The 1835 Article on Marriage, which stayed in the Doctrine and Covenants until 1876, declared one man and one wife. Church organs repeatedly denied 'spiritual wifery' throughout the Nauvoo period, while the practice spread secretly among the leadership. John 8:44, Ephesians 4:25, Proverbs 12:22 and Colossians 3:9 are the texts critics apply.
js-polygamy-denials.response: FAIR argues that the denials were carefully worded. Smith denied adultery, and he denied John C. Bennett's freelance 'spiritual wifery' — not divinely sanctioned celestial marriage. He had only one legal wife, so 'I can only find one' was technically true. Disclosure would have brought mob violence and prosecution, as the Expositor episode proved, so concealment protected the community. Apologists draw an analogy to Abraham's misdirection about Sarah. The church's own essay acknowledges the secrecy, and says that participants found it agonizing.
js-polygamy-denials.rationale: The denials and the concurrent marriages are both documented beyond dispute. The apologetic defense concedes the deception and argues justification for it. Technically worded statements made with intent to create a false impression are still deception, by any ordinary or biblical standard of truth-telling. That is the claim being graded here.

eternal-polygamy-today.claim: Serial eternal polygamy is current practice. A widowed man may be sealed to an additional wife while remaining sealed to his deceased wife. Two church presidents are in that position. Russell M. Nelson was sealed to Wendy Watson in 2006, after Dantzel's death. Dallin H. Oaks was sealed to Kristen McMain in 2000, after June's death. Each is sealed to two women for eternity. A living woman cannot be sealed to a second man without cancelling the first sealing. D&C 132:61-63 has never been de-canonized. Carol Lynn Pearson's research documents the resulting grief among believing Latter-day Saint women who expect to be shared in eternity. Matthew 22:30 and 1 Timothy 3:2 are the texts critics cite.
eternal-polygamy-today.response: Dallin H. Oaks addressed this directly in General Conference in October 2019. The church makes no doctrinal claim about family configuration in the next life. Trust in the Lord: sealing complexities will be resolved by a loving God, and no one will receive an eternal arrangement they do not want. Since 1998, deceased women may be sealed by proxy to all the men they married in life, on the assumption that the woman will choose. The restriction on living women is administrative, not a statement of eternal inequality. And the church has not practised plural marriage since 1904; it excommunicates those who do.
eternal-polygamy-today.rationale: The sealing asymmetry, the leaders' own second sealings, and the canonical status of D&C 132 are all matters of public record and current Handbook policy. The apologetic response is a candid 'we don't know.' That mitigates the pastoral weight, but it refutes nothing. The asymmetry between men's sealings and living women's sealings remains in force.

polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.claim: The church's Gospel Topics essay 'Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo' concedes that Joseph Smith told women an angel appeared three times commanding polygamy. In the final appearance 'the angel came with a drawn sword, threatening Joseph with destruction unless he went forward.' He deployed this account in proposals. Zina Diantha Huntington was proposed to while courting Henry Jacobs, and was sealed to Joseph after being told of the angel; Henry later stood as a witness. Mary Elizabeth Rollins Lightner was already married. Lucy Walker was 16, living in his home after her mother's death; she was told to seek confirmation, and later described her anguish. Helen Mar Kimball, aged 14, recorded Joseph's promise: 'If you will take this step, it will ensure your eternal salvation and exaltation, and that of your father's household.' D&C 132 canonizes the pattern, since wives who refuse are 'destroyed' at verses 54 and 64. Scripture warns that even an angel preaching another gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8), and that Satan appears as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.response: Brian Hales and FAIR argue that the angel accounts originate with faithful participants, and that they demonstrate Joseph's reluctance. He delayed for years and acted only under divine compulsion, which is the opposite of a predator's eagerness. They note that Helen Mar Kimball's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic — an 'eternity-only' linking of families for the next life. They note that women such as Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley refused Joseph without spiritual penalty, which shows real agency. And they argue that mid-nineteenth-century marriage norms for young women differed sharply from today's, so modern categories of coercion are anachronistic.
polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.rationale: The essential facts are conceded in the church's own essay: the drawn-sword angel, Helen's marriage 'several months before her 15th birthday,' and the sealings to already-married women. The salvation promise to Helen comes from her own faithful memoir. The destruction threats of D&C 132 are canon. The apologetic reframing disputes interpretation, not substance. And 'an angel threatened him into it' is itself the admission. The proposals bundled divine reward with divine threat, which is coercion by any biblical test, and Galatians 1:8 addresses precisely the scenario of angelic authorization for another gospel. The severity is high because it goes to the prophet's character and to the fruit test of Matthew 7:15-20.

post-manifesto-polygamy.claim: The 1890 Manifesto, now Official Declaration 1, publicly announced the end of plural marriage. Church leaders repeatedly denied any new plural marriages thereafter. In fact apostles and members of the First Presidency secretly authorized or performed roughly 250 new plural marriages between 1890 and 1904. That is D. Michael Quinn's count in Dialogue 18:1 in 1985; B. Carmon Hardy documents 262 in the appendix to Solemn Covenant. Many took place in Mexico, in Canada, or at sea. Nine or ten General Authorities themselves took new plural wives. The Reed Smoot Senate hearings of 1904 to 1907 exposed the practice. In March 1904, church president Joseph F. Smith testified under oath that he had continued to cohabit with his five plural wives, and had fathered eleven children with them since 1890, in acknowledged violation of the law. Weeks later he issued the 1904 Second Manifesto. It asserted that no post-1890 marriages had occurred 'with the sanction, consent or knowledge of the Church' — a claim contradicted by the documented participation of his own counselors and apostles. Apostles John W. Taylor and Matthias F. Cowley were forced from the Quorum of the Twelve over the affair. This repeats the Nauvoo pattern of 1841 to 1844, making it the second sustained episode of public institutional denial of a privately continued practice.
post-manifesto-polygamy.response: The church's own Gospel Topics essay supplies the steelman and concedes most of the record. 'After October 1890, plural marriages continued to be quietly performed' in Mexico and Canada. 'The Manifesto declared President Woodruff's intention to submit to the laws of the United States. It said nothing about the laws of other nations.' Leaders in good faith read it as a legally scoped document, not a revelation banning the principle worldwide. 'Many Church leaders believed the Manifesto merely suspended plural marriage for an indefinite time.' Existing husbands 'continued to cohabit with their plural wives and fathered children with them well into the 20th century,' rather than abandon covenant families. Only with the 1904 Second Manifesto were members 'put on notice that new plural marriages stood unapproved by God and the Church,' after which Taylor and Cowley 'were eventually dropped from the quorum.' Apologists add that moving away from a practice leaders believed divinely commanded was wrenching, that it was conducted under federal persecution, and that ambiguity rather than conspiracy explains the fifteen-year lag.
post-manifesto-polygamy.rationale: This is the rare case where the church's own essay concedes nearly every element of the critical claim. Post-Manifesto plural marriages were quietly performed with leader involvement. Cohabitation and child-fathering continued. The Manifesto's legal scope was deliberately limited. Two apostles were removed. And Joseph F. Smith's sworn Smoot testimony is a first-person presidential admission. What the steelman reframes is sincere ambiguity against duplicity. It cannot erase that leaders publicly and repeatedly denied what they privately authorized — including the Second Manifesto's 'sanction, consent or knowledge' claim, falsified by Quinn's and Hardy's documentation. Nor that this replays the Nauvoo denial pattern. Measured by Proverbs 12:22, Ephesians 4:25 and Numbers 30:2, the institutional pattern stands conceded in substance and contested only in motive.

avoid-87-wives-overclaim.claim: The popular version says Joseph Smith had 87 wives. Sometimes 50-plus, sometimes hundreds.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim.response: The documented count is about 30 to 40, and that number is the church's own. The Gospel Topics essay says 'careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40,' citing Brian Hales. Todd Compton documents 33. Higher figures — Stanley Ivins once tallied 84 — pad the list with unverifiable and posthumous sealings. Claiming 87 lets an apologist correct your arithmetic and walk away from the substance.
avoid-87-wives-overclaim.rationale: Overclaiming is the one gift you can give FAIR on this topic. The church-admitted facts need no inflation. Thirty to forty wives. One aged 14 — Helen Mar Kimball, 'sealed months before her 15th birthday,' in the essay's own words. Roughly a dozen already married to living husbands. And public denials throughout. Every clause is sourced to the church's own essay, and covered by this site's other polygamy cases. Say 'thirty to forty — that's your church's number, footnoted to its own website,' and nothing can be rebutted.

avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.claim: The popular version says Mormons still practise polygamy today, with prairie dresses and plural households in view.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.response: That is false for the mainstream church. Since the 1904 Second Manifesto, contracting or solemnizing a plural marriage gets a member excommunicated. Today's practising polygamists — the FLDS, the AUB and various independents — are splinter groups the Latter-day Saint church denounces. The prairie-dress image is FLDS, not LDS.
avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.rationale: Confusing the Latter-day Saints with the FLDS is the fastest way to get politely dismissed. But drop the claim about mortal practice and the doctrinal one stands untouched. D&C 132 remains canonized scripture. Widowed men are sealed eternally to more than one wife today; Presidents Nelson and Oaks are each eternally sealed to two women. And the church's own history shows leaders secretly authorizing plural marriages for fourteen years after the 1890 Manifesto. Say: 'You're right, no one practises it now — so why is the revelation commanding it still in your scriptures, and why is eternal polygamy still live in your sealing policy?'

priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.claim: From Brigham Young's announcements in 1852 until Official Declaration 2 in June 1978, the church barred members of Black African descent. Men could not be ordained to the priesthood. Men and women could not receive the temple endowment or be sealed. In the church's own soteriology, that meant exclusion from the ordinances required for exaltation, for 126 years. First Presidency statements in 1949 and 1969 defended the ban as divinely instituted, grounding it in premortal conduct and in the curse of Cain. The church's 2013 essay 'Race and the Priesthood' now disavows 'the theories advanced in the past.' It situates the ban's origin in the racial culture of 1850s America, and claims no founding revelation. Critics set the policy against Peter's revelation that 'God is no respecter of persons' (Acts 10:34-35), and Paul's 'there is neither Jew nor Greek… ye are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28). Acts 17:26, Colossians 3:11 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.response: The steelmanned response leans on the 2013 essay itself. Joseph Smith ordained Black men — Elijah Able and Q. Walker Lewis. The restriction arose under Young, amid 1850s American racial culture, without a recorded founding revelation. It was ended by genuine revelation to Spencer W. Kimball in 1978. And the church has since repudiated every theological justification it once offered. Apologists draw the parallel of Acts itself: the gospel was withheld from Gentiles until Peter's revelation. God lifts restrictions on his own timetable, through living prophets. And a church capable of disavowing its leaders' errors demonstrates ongoing revelation rather than disproving it.
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.rationale: The history is fully documented and conceded in the church's own essay. The Acts 10 parallel cuts against the defense rather than for it. Peter's revelation abolished ethnic exclusion at the church's founding. The Latter-day Saint ban was instituted after an inclusive start, defended as doctrine by prophets for over a century, and its stated justifications are now officially disavowed. That leaves the problem of prophetic reliability intact.

mountain-meadows-massacre.claim: On 11 September 1857, Mormon militiamen of the Iron County brigade lured the surrendered Baker-Fancher wagon train out under a white flag and murdered about 120 men, women and children, sparing only the small children. The attack was planned and ordered by local church and militia leaders in the Cedar City area, including the stake president Isaac Haight and Bishop John D. Lee. The church's own sponsored history — Ronald Walker, Richard Turley and Glen Leonard, 'Massacre at Mountain Meadows,' Oxford 2008 — confirms local church leadership responsibility. In 2007, Elder Henry B. Eyring expressed 'profound regret' on behalf of the First Presidency. Only John D. Lee was ever executed, in 1877. Exodus 20:13, Matthew 5:44 and Romans 12:19 are the texts at issue.
mountain-meadows-massacre.response: The church fully acknowledges the massacre and its horror. The steelman is context. It occurred amid Utah War hysteria: a federal army was approaching, memories of the Missouri and Nauvoo persecutions were fresh, and wartime rhetoric was everywhere. The church-sponsored history concludes that Brigham Young did not order it. His express letter counselling that the train be allowed to pass arrived two days late. Local leaders acted against counsel, and the cover-up was local before it was institutional. Participants were later excommunicated. The church has built memorials, cooperated with descendant groups, and published the fullest account itself.
mountain-meadows-massacre.rationale: The massacre, its scale, and the orchestration by local church leadership are established by the church's own sponsored scholarship and official statements. Critics who claim Brigham Young directly ordered it go beyond the documentary evidence; the church history concludes he did not, though his war-hysteria preaching contributed. The claim as stated — that church leaders at the Cedar City level planned mass murder — is conceded by all serious parties.

blood-atonement.claim: Brigham Young taught from the Tabernacle pulpit that some sins exceed the atoning power of Christ's blood and require the sinner's own. 'There are sins that men commit for which they cannot receive forgiveness in this world, or in that which is to come, and if they had their eyes open to see their true condition, they would be perfectly willing to have their blood spilt upon the ground, that the smoke thereof might ascend to heaven as an offering for their sins.' That is Journal of Discourses 4:53-54, from 1856; see also 4:219-220, from 1857. In June 2010 the church formally stated that 'so-called blood atonement… is not a doctrine of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.' Scripture teaches the total sufficiency of Christ's one sacrifice: 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (Hebrews 10:12-14); 'the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin' (1 John 1:7); 'It is finished' (John 19:30). Hebrews 9:26, Isaiah 53:5-6 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6 say the same.
blood-atonement.response: FAIR and Mormonr answer on four fronts. Blood-atonement rhetoric belongs to the overheated preaching of the Mormon Reformation of 1856 and 1857, and was hyperbole aimed at provoking repentance. It was framed as voluntary, and tied to a theory of capital punishment for capital crimes echoing Genesis 9:6, not to vigilante practice; there is no evidence the church ever institutionalized killing sinners to save them. It was never canonized — D&C 42:18 and 42:79 prescribe excommunication and civil justice, not ritual death. And the church has repeatedly and officially repudiated it, in Bruce R. McConkie's 1978 letter and in the 2010 statement. It stands today as an abandoned nineteenth-century speculation.
blood-atonement.rationale: Both the teaching and its disavowal are documented beyond dispute. The sermons are verbatim in the Journal of Discourses, and the 2010 statement shows the church understands what was taught well enough to disavow it by name. What Young preached — that certain sins lie beyond the reach of Christ's blood — is a direct verbal contradiction of Hebrews 10:14 and 1 John 1:7. The hyperbole steelman strains against Young's own words, which read as sober counsel across multiple sermons and years. The severity is graded medium because the doctrine is genuinely repudiated and carries no current weight in salvation. Its enduring force is as a second clear case, alongside Adam-God, of a prophet teaching over the pulpit what the church now calls false doctrine. That bears on the reliability of the prophetic office.

abuse-helpline-2022.claim: A 2022 Associated Press investigation, drawing on about 12,000 pages of sealed records, reported that the church's abuse help line routes bishops' reports of child sexual abuse to church lawyers at Kirton McConkie rather than to police. In the Bisbee, Arizona case, Paul Adams confessed abuse of his daughter to two bishops beginning in 2011. Church counsel advised that Arizona's clergy-penitent privilege barred reporting. The abuse continued for roughly seven more years, and came to include a second daughter, an infant, until Adams was independently caught in 2017. Critics allege that the help line functions to manage legal risk ahead of child protection. Mark 9:42, Luke 8:17 and James 1:27 are the texts they cite.
abuse-helpline-2022.response: The church calls the AP framing egregiously wrong. The bishop repeatedly urged Adams and his wife to report, and tried to intervene. Arizona law made the confession privileged, meaning the bishop legally could not report information derived from confession without consent. Arizona's courts agreed; in 2023 the state supreme court upheld the privilege and dismissed the claims against the church. The help line exists so that untrained lay bishops immediately reach professionals who instruct them to comply with reporting laws, which vary by state. The church says its first priority is protecting victims. And the abuse was known to others — the mother, and people who saw what Adams posted online — who also failed to report.
abuse-helpline-2022.rationale: The core timeline is established by court records and is undisputed: a confession in 2011, no report, and seven more years of abuse. The claim about cause and culpability — that the help line exists to protect the institution ahead of children — is genuinely contested. The legal advice tracked Arizona's actual privilege statute, the courts sided with the church, and the bishops' constrained position is real. What remains unrefuted is that the system's design produced a catastrophic outcome, and that help-line calls route through defense counsel. Whether that is malice, negligence or legal compliance is the contested question.

oath-of-vengeance.claim: From roughly 1845 until about 1927, the temple endowment included a covenant to 'pray and never cease to pray Almighty God to avenge the blood of the prophets upon this nation, and… teach the same to your children and to your children's children unto the third and fourth generation.' Its existence and wording were documented under oath in the United States Senate's Reed Smoot hearings of 1904 to 1906. It was quietly removed around 1927, during the church's assimilation era, with no public explanation and no repudiation. Matthew 5:44, Romans 12:19-21 and Luke 23:34 are the texts at issue.
oath-of-vengeance.response: FAIR emphasizes that the oath asked God to avenge. It did not commit members to take vengeance themselves. That closely parallels the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:10 — 'How long, O Lord… dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?' — and the imprecatory Psalms. It arose in the raw aftermath of the state-tolerated murders of Joseph and Hyrum Smith, for which no one was ever convicted, and it was removed as the wounds healed. Temple ceremonies have always been revised, and its removal reflects the living, adaptive nature of the ordinances.
oath-of-vengeance.rationale: The oath's existence, its wording, its eighty-year duration and its 1927 removal are established by sworn Senate testimony and by peer-reviewed scholarship, including David John Buerger's work in Dialogue. No informed apologist denies that it existed. The Revelation 6:10 parallel is a genuinely fair mitigation of the caricature that this was an oath to commit violence. But the documented claim stands: a multigenerational vengeance prayer against the United States, embedded in the faith's holiest ordinance, set against Jesus's command to pray for enemies.

danites-1838.claim: In Missouri in 1838, a secret Mormon paramilitary band called the Danites was organized under Sampson Avard. It intimidated and expelled church dissenters; the Danite Manifesto threatened Oliver Cowdery, the Whitmers and others. During the conflict of October 1838, Mormon forces including Danites raided and burned the non-Mormon settlements of Gallatin and Millport. The contested question is how much Joseph Smith knew and authorized. Avard testified that Smith was the mastermind. Stephen LeSueur argues that Smith endorsed the Danites and benefited from them. Church-aligned scholars argue that Avard ran his own criminal program. Romans 12:17-19 and 2 Corinthians 10:3-4 are the texts at issue.
danites-1838.response: Avard was a self-aggrandizing opportunist who turned state's witness to save himself, which makes his 'Smith was the mastermind' testimony maximally self-serving. He was excommunicated in 1839. Leland Gentry and Alexander Baugh trace three phases: legitimate community defense, which Avard then corrupted into secret oaths and plunder without Smith's authorization. The 1838 context was existential. Mormons were being burned out, and were shortly subject to Governor Boggs's Extermination Order and the Haun's Mill massacre. Mormon violence, while real, was a fraction of what was inflicted on them. The church's own history topics acknowledge Danite excesses.
danites-1838.rationale: The Danites' existence, the expulsions of dissenters, and the raids are undisputed. The load-bearing claim — Smith's personal authorization — rests substantially on Avard's compromised testimony, and serious historians genuinely divide, LeSueur against Gentry and Baugh. Smith publicly praised Danite leaders and rode the wave, but operational command is not established. Contested is the honest grade.

nauvoo-expositor-carthage.claim: On 10 June 1844, Joseph Smith as mayor and the Nauvoo city council ordered the destruction of the Nauvoo Expositor's press, after its single issue of 7 June. That issue's core reporting — on Smith's secret plural marriage and on his plurality-of-gods teaching — was substantively accurate. The destruction triggered riot charges, Smith's surrender at Carthage, and the mob attack of 27 June. At Carthage, Smith fired a smuggled six-shot pepperbox pistol into the mob, wounding three men. That is John Taylor's own account, in History of the Church 7:102-103, and it was long omitted from devotional retellings of the 'martyrdom.' 1 Peter 2:23, Matthew 26:52 and Proverbs 10:9 are the texts at issue.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.response: Dallin H. Oaks published a legal analysis in the Utah Law Review in 1965. Before the Fourteenth Amendment, the First Amendment did not bind city governments, and abating the newspaper as a nuisance had colorable legal basis under the Nauvoo Charter — though Oaks concedes that destroying the press itself was likely beyond legal justification. The council feared the paper would incite mob violence against the city, and the mob came anyway. On Carthage: defending oneself against a lynch mob with painted faces does not negate an unjust killing. Smith was in state custody under the governor's pledged protection. The pistol is recorded by the eyewitness John Taylor himself, and the church has published the fact, including in Saints. Martyrdom in the broad sense means being killed for one's religion, not dying passively.
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.rationale: Every factual element is documented in the Joseph Smith Papers, in History of the Church, and in the church's own topic essays: the accuracy of the Expositor's reporting, the mayor-ordered destruction, and the pepperbox. Apologetics contests the framing — martyr against gunfight victim — and mitigates the legality question. But the killing was unambiguously extrajudicial murder, and the suppression of a truthful press was the proximate trigger. Both things are true. Neither is refuted.

policy-of-exclusion-2015.claim: In November 2015 the church's Handbook was changed. Members in same-sex marriages were labelled 'apostates' subject to mandatory discipline, and their children were barred from baby blessings and baptism until age 18. Baptism was then conditioned on disavowing their parents' marriage and leaving their home. In January 2016, President Russell M. Nelson publicly declared the policy a revelation — 'the mind of the Lord and the will of the Lord,' revealed to President Monson. In April 2019 the church reversed both provisions, also framing the reversal as directed by the Lord. A revelation was reversed by revelation within four years, and families bore the cost in between. Deuteronomy 24:16, Ezekiel 18:20, Mark 10:14 and Numbers 23:19 are the texts critics cite.
policy-of-exclusion-2015.response: The church frames both the policy and its reversal as inspired responses to circumstances. Neither, on that view, is eternal doctrine. The 2015 policy aimed to protect children from being caught between home and church. The same reasoning already applied to the children of polygamists. By 2019, leaders concluded through continued revelation that it caused more harm than it prevented. Continuing revelation allows course correction by its nature. Apologists cite Acts 10 as the template, where the exclusion of Gentiles is reversed. Policies carry out doctrine for a time and a place. The doctrine of marriage beneath them never changed.
policy-of-exclusion-2015.rationale: Every fact is on the record. That includes Nelson's own 'will of the Lord' framing. It forecloses the easier defense, that the 2015 change was policy and never revelation. The argument that continuing revelation can reverse course is coherent on its own terms. But it concedes the documented sequence rather than refuting it. What a four-year reversal implies about revelation is for the reader. The record itself is not in dispute.

quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.claim: To resign your membership you normally go through your bishop, and then the stake president. There are waiting periods. Leaders reach out to you. Many people who resign say the visits and calls went on, even after they asked to be left alone. Mark Naugle, a Utah lawyer, set up a free service called QuitMormon.com. It sends the demand as a lawyer, so the church has to deal with him rather than with the member. It has handled on the order of 150,000 resignations since 2015. In 2019 the church said those submissions must be notarized, citing fake requests. That added one more step.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.response: The General Handbook already sets out a free official path. A member writes to the bishop and asks that the record be removed. The request is to be honoured. Leaders are told to check who the person is, and to make sure they know what follows. The church says those steps guard against fake or rushed removals. It says the 2019 notary rule came after real fake requests, including pranks that resigned other people. Follow-up contact is care from lay leaders, who are taught to answer with love and not to pester. And any member may simply stop coming, with no penalty at all.
quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.rationale: The facts hold up. The scale of QuitMormon has been reported in the mainstream press. Both sides confirm the 2019 notary rule. And the reports of contact after leaving are many. A legal buffer is the whole point of the service, and it exists because of them. What is argued here is motive: care for the member, or pressure to keep them.

temple-wedding-family-exclusion.claim: Only members holding a current temple recommend may attend a temple sealing. So family who are not members, or who have resigned, or who do not hold a recommend, must wait outside during the wedding. That includes a bride's or groom's own parents.
