Until May 2019, couples in the United States who held a civil ceremony first — so that excluded family could attend — were penalized with a one-year wait before sealing. That pressured couples to choose the temple over excluded relatives. The First Presidency removed the one-year penalty in 2019, explicitly citing families feeling excluded. The recommend requirement for attending sealings is unchanged.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion.response: The church holds that the temple is a sacred space whose ordinances require covenant worthiness. It is the same standard applied to every attendee for any temple ordinance, and it is not aimed at wedding guests. The 2019 First Presidency change was made expressly so that 'when a temple marriage would cause parents or immediate family members to feel excluded, a civil marriage followed by a temple sealing is authorized.' Couples may now hold a fully inclusive civil wedding first and be sealed immediately after. The church presents that as resolving the family-exclusion dilemma while preserving the sanctity of the temple.
temple-wedding-family-exclusion.rationale: The exclusion rule and the pre-2019 one-year penalty are documented church policy. The church's own 2019 letter acknowledges the family-exclusion harm it was mitigating. The 2019 change is a genuine improvement. It confirms the underlying factual claim rather than refuting it.

byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.claim: BYU asks every student for a yearly sign-off from a church leader. It calls this an ecclesiastical endorsement. BYU's own written policy says the sign-off is pulled at once if a student is excommunicated, disfellowshipped, or resigns. Losing it costs a great deal. Good Honor Code standing. The right to stay enrolled. A job on campus. A room on campus. Even the degree itself, if the course work is done. So a student who stops believing in the middle of a degree faces being thrown out, or years of hiding it. Students who were never members may attend, at a higher fee. A member who leaves is therefore treated worse than someone who was never baptized. FreeBYU took the matter to the accrediting bodies and lost. A narrow appeal route was added in 2015 and 2016.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.response: BYU says it is a private religious school, paid for in large part by tithing. Latter-day Saint students pay a much lower fee, and the faith community makes up the rest. The deal is stated up front: stay in good standing with the church that funds you. Students agree to it when they enrol. BYU notes that the accrediting bodies and the American Bar Association have upheld its right to set religious terms. An appeal route now exists for students who resign. And every student needs the yearly sign-off, including those who are not members. They just do not need to be members.
byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.rationale: The policy is set out word for word in BYU's own papers. Leaving the church pulls the sign-off, and pulling the sign-off ends the right to stay. So the facts come from the school itself. What is really in dispute is what to call it. A private school setting religious terms, or a penalty for changing your mind.

social-costs-shunning.claim: People who leave often report strain in a marriage, being cut off by family, losing their community, and being pushed to the edge. Those patterns are set out in reporting at NPR and HuffPost, and in thousands of gathered accounts. Two things drive them. First, Latter-day Saint teaching: a family split by faith loses the hope of being sealed for ever. Second, the word 'apostate' carries heavy weight. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk named 'so-called scholars,' feminists and gays as the church's three dangers, and that shaped the mood. Note one thing. Unlike the Jehovah's Witnesses, this church has no formal rule to shun. So the costs are social and family ones, not ones the church orders.
social-costs-shunning.response: Church leaders have spoken against cutting off family who leave, more than once and by name. Elder D. Todd Christofferson said in public that he 'would not cut that child out of family life.' Official teaching tells members to keep loving and including family who go. There is no teaching, handbook rule, or discipline that tells a member to shun. The church would add that broken ties follow a change of faith in many traditions, and that this is how families behave rather than what the church asks.
social-costs-shunning.rationale: The costs themselves are well attested, in reporting and in a great mass of first-hand accounts. The harder claim is that the church causes them, and that one is genuinely argued. The written policy tells members not to shun. The teaching and the rhetoric can still push people apart. Both things are true at once: the harm is real, and there is no order to shun.

grenfell-exit-testimony.claim: Alyssa Grenfell went to BYU. She now writes and posts as an ex-Mormon, with about 570,000 subscribers on YouTube. Her 2023 book is 'How to Leave the Mormon Church: An Exmormon's Guide to Rebuilding After Religion.' In it, and on her channel, she sets out three things. Members who step away keep being contacted and visited by ward representatives. Wearing the garment each day works as a check on the body, so giving it up is a signal others can see, and it costs you. And pulling a faith apart costs you your sense of self, your family and your friends. Her book is one person's testimony. Its central facts are backed up elsewhere. Contact after leaving matches what the resignation cases show, and garment rules are set out in the church's own General Handbook at 38.5.
grenfell-exit-testimony.response: The church does not answer memoirs by former members. Its standing position is that a member who steps away is still loved and still welcome. Ministering visits are freely given care, and they stop when a person asks, or resigns. The garment is a sacred private covenant, taken freely in the temple. It is not a way of watching anyone. Apologists would add that a paid ex-Mormon media career has its own pull, and that one life should not stand in for a church of 17 million.
grenfell-exit-testimony.rationale: Her main claims hold up at the level of pattern. Contact after leaving, garment rules, and the social cost of going are all backed by church papers and by outside reporting. The book itself is one person's word on particular events, and it is badged that way here. It belongs on the site as a voice for a pattern that is documented. It does not stand as proof on its own.

ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.claim: Jeremy Runnells' CES Letter of 2013 compiled a list of historical problems and sent it to a Church Educational System director, who never answered. It became the most widely circulated exit document in modern Mormonism. Runnells was summoned to a disciplinary council and resigned in 2016. In the same period the church published 13 Gospel Topics Essays, between 2013 and 2015, conceding many long-denied historical facts — multiple First Vision accounts, seer-stone translation, and Joseph Smith's polygamy. They were released with no announcement, unsigned, and buried in the website's topics database. Church Historian Elder Steven E. Snow acknowledged the deliberate 'soft roll out.' In some cases, members teaching from the essays were rebuked by local leaders.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.response: The church's steelman is that it did the historically unprecedented thing critics demanded. It published frank, scholar-vetted essays on its hardest topics on its own website, and later integrated that history into the official 'Saints' volumes and the curriculum. Elder Snow's explanation of the quiet rollout was pastoral rather than conspiratorial. Most members were not troubled by these issues, and the essays were placed where searching members would find them without alarming those who were not asking. FAIR argues that the CES Letter itself is a shotgun compilation of recycled claims, most of which the essays and the apologetic literature substantively answer.
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.rationale: The factual timeline is established, including by Elder Snow's own recorded explanation of the deliberate low-visibility release. Whether this is 'information control' or 'pastoral prudence' is an interpretive dispute, and the church did ultimately publish the material. Runnells' discipline for compiling questions, however, is documented, and it sits uneasily with the transparency claim.

september-six.claim: In September 1993, six Mormon scholars and feminists were cut off or disfellowshipped within weeks of each other. They were Lavina Fielding Anderson, Avraham Gileadi, Maxine Hanks, D. Michael Quinn, Paul Toscano and Lynne Kanavel Whitesides. What they had done was publish history and theology that leaders did not want. Quinn had written on plural marriage after 1890. Others had written on Heavenly Mother, or argued for women. Months before, the apostle Boyd K. Packer had named the church's three great dangers in public: 'the gay-lesbian movement, the feminist movement, and the so-called scholars or intellectuals.' The discipline was local on paper, but the evidence points to apostles taking part. Mormon studies went quiet for a generation.
september-six.response: FAIR and the church hold that discipline is run locally, by stake presidents. It is for conduct such as speaking out against the church and its leaders. That is apostasy as the handbook sets it out, and it is not scholarship as such. They note that many working historians publish critical work and are never disciplined, and that the church does not run these councils from the centre. The church also points to what came after, as a sign that it can take rigorous history: the Joseph Smith Papers, the Gospel Topics Essays, and Maxine Hanks being rebaptized in 2012.
september-six.rationale: The six actions, their timing, and Packer's speech about three dangers are all on the record. No one disputes them. What is argued is only how much was run from the centre. As a claim about how the church met dissent, it stands.

sec-ensign-peak-settlement.claim: On 21 February 2023 the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the church and its investment arm, Ensign Peak Advisors. The charge was failing to disclose. From 1997 to 2019, Ensign Peak hid a portfolio of listed shares behind 13 shell LLCs with named-only 'managers.' It filed Forms 13F that were wrong, so that the church's holdings would not show. The portfolio grew to about $32 billion. Per the SEC order, this was done with the knowledge and approval of the church's First Presidency, out of concern about bad press. Ensign Peak paid $4 million and the church paid $1 million to settle. This is a legal finding about candour. It is not a claim about whether any doctrine is true.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement.response: The church's official statement says it took legal advice on how to meet the 13F rules while keeping the portfolio private. It cites scripture on keeping sacred gifts quiet and on avoiding show. It says it regrets the mistakes made. When the SEC first raised a concern in 2019, Ensign Peak changed its filings at once. It now files a single form for the whole fund. The church stresses what the settlement did not allege. No misuse of funds. No fraud against investors. No harm to members. It was a reporting-form breach, and the money is still set aside for the church's religious and charitable work.
sec-ensign-peak-settlement.rationale: The facts are fixed by the SEC order, and by the church's own settlement and public statement owning the mistakes. The shell companies, and the wish to avoid bad press, are in the order itself. All that is left to argue is what to call it: poor legal advice, or a choice to hide.

tithing-enforcement.claim: Temple recommends are required for the ordinances the church teaches are necessary for exaltation, including attending a child's temple wedding. They are conditioned on answering 'Are you a full-tithe payer?' in a worthiness interview. An annual 'tithing settlement' — renamed 'tithing declaration' in 2019 — has members declare their status to the bishop. 'Fire insurance' rhetoric flows from canonized D&C 64:23, 'he that is tithed shall not be burned at his coming,' with the standard set at D&C 119:3-4. Leaders have taught paying tithing before feeding one's family. James Huntsman's fraud suit over the use of tithing was dismissed 11-0 by the en banc Ninth Circuit in January 2025. Critics set the structure against 2 Corinthians 9:7, Matthew 23:23 and Mark 12:41-44.
tithing-enforcement.response: The church has no paid local clergy. Bishops, teachers and leaders all serve free, so tithing funds operations, chapels, temples, education, and a large welfare and humanitarian programme. Members widely testify that tithing is a blessing rather than extortion. Tithing also predates Mormonism: Malachi 3:8-10 frames non-payment as robbing God, so the gating standard is arguably biblical. The Huntsman ruling vindicated the church's statements, since the court found no misrepresentation — City Creek was funded from earnings on invested reserves, exactly as President Hinckley had said. And declaration is self-reported; no one audits income.
tithing-enforcement.rationale: The recommend question, the declaration meeting, D&C 64:23 and the exaltation-gating structure are all in current church publications. None of it is contested. The critics' strongest overreach, the fraud theory, was judicially answered 11-0 and is graded accordingly. But the core claim is simply a description of current practice: ordinances critical to salvation are conditioned on a financial contribution, which sits against 2 Corinthians 9:7's 'not grudgingly, or of necessity.'

missionary-program-realities.claim: Latter-day Saint missionaries go out young. Men at 18 for 24 months, women at 19 for 18 months. They work full-time and unpaid, and they pay to do it. The flat sum has been $500 a month since 2020, and families usually find it. Missionaries hand over control of the day to mission rules and a mission president. That covers the schedule, what they may read and watch, and a companion at all times. Until February 2019, contact with family was weekly email and two phone calls a year, on Mother's Day and at Christmas. The pull to serve, from family and from culture, is strong. So is the stigma of coming home early. Members write about both at length.
missionary-program-realities.response: Service is freely chosen, and it is framed as consecrated service rather than work. The flat payment levels it out: a missionary in Tokyo pays what one in Peru pays, and ward funds cover those who cannot. Huge numbers of returned missionaries call it the making of them — a language learned, a habit of discipline, a life of service. The rules exist for safety and focus, as they do in monastic and military life. And the 2019 changes, with weekly calls and looser schedules, show the church listening to how missionaries fare.
missionary-program-realities.rationale: Every element comes from the church's own publications: the cost, the rules, and the twice-a-year call policy before 2019. The steelman is real. It is freely chosen, and the benefits people report are genuine. Calling it unpaid labour understates how much people want to go. But the claim describes facts the church itself confirms. The severity is low because the practice is open, and consented to.

jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.claim: Latter-day Saint scripture and manuals teach that Lucifer was 'a spirit son of God.' In the premortal council he offered a rival plan of redemption — 'Behold, here am I, send me, I will be thy son… wherefore give me thine honor' (Moses 4:1-4) — competing with the premortal Jesus before the world was made (Abraham 3:27-28; D&C 76:25-27; Gospel Principles chapter 3). Since all beings are spirit children of the same Heavenly Father, Jesus and Lucifer are, in that taxonomy, elder and younger spirit brothers. The church's own Newsroom statement of December 2007, answering Mike Huckabee, acknowledged the underlying doctrine while rejecting the framing: all beings 'were created by God and are his spirit children,' while 'Satan… is a fallen angel.' Biblically, Christ is the Creator of all spiritual beings — 'by him were all things created… whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers' (Colossians 1:16). Satan is therefore a creature Christ made, of a different order from his Maker; Ezekiel 28:13-15 says 'thou wast created.' John 1:3, Hebrews 1:4-6 and Nehemiah 9:6 say the same.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.response: FAIR concedes the taxonomy is 'technically accurate' but calls the framing misleading without context. Shared spirit-parentage implies no parity, any more than Cain and Abel's brotherhood makes them equals. FAIR notes that the Bible itself calls Satan one of the 'sons of God' at Job 1:6 and 2:1. Jesus is uniquely 'the first and greatest Son,' the Creator of this world, and the Only Begotten in the flesh, while Satan squandered his potential and became the eternal enemy of God. The 2007 Newsroom statement takes the same line: Christ and Satan are 'diametrically opposite' in every attribute.
jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.rationale: The doctrine is documented from the canon (Moses 4; Abraham 3), from the current manual, and from the church's own 2007 statement, which confirms rather than denies the shared spirit-parentage. The steelman rebuts the crude version — that Mormons think Jesus and the devil are alike — but it does not touch the actual conflict. That conflict is about what kind of being each is, not about morals. In biblical Christology, Satan belongs to the class of created 'principalities and powers' that Christ himself made. Creator and fallen creature can no more be brothers of one species than a potter and his pot. Job 1:6's 'sons of God' designates angelic creatures in Yahweh's court, not begotten siblings of Yahweh. The moral-asymmetry defense answers a charge nobody serious is making, and leaves the category collapse intact.

god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.claim: Joseph Smith taught canonically that 'The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's' (D&C 130:22; see also 131:7-8). In the King Follett discourse of 1844 he preached that 'God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man.' The church's current essay 'Becoming Like God' still quotes that approvingly, alongside Lorenzo Snow's couplet, and affirms Smith's rejection of creation from nothing: God 'organized the universe out of existing elements' (Abraham 3:22-24; 4:1). The trajectory reached its extreme in Brigham Young's Adam-God doctrine — 'Adam is our father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do' (Journal of Discourses 1:50-51, 1852), incorporated into the 1877 temple lecture at the veil. President Spencer W. Kimball officially repudiated it in October 1976: 'We denounce that theory… false doctrine.' The Bible teaches the opposite at every point. 'God is a Spirit' (John 4:24). 'God is not a man' (Numbers 23:19; Hosea 11:9). 'From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God' (Psalm 90:2). 'Before me there was no God formed' (Isaiah 43:10; cf. 45:5, Malachi 3:6). And the worlds were framed by the word of God (Hebrews 11:3).
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.response: FAIR argues that 'God is a Spirit' at John 4:24 is a statement of mode and character, not anatomy. It parallels 'God is light' at 1 John 1:5 and 'a consuming fire' at Deuteronomy 4:24, which nobody takes as exhaustive. Spirit and embodiment are compatible in any case, since resurrected beings have bodies of flesh and bone at Luke 24:39. FAIR marshals the theophanies of Exodus 33:11 and 33:23, and notes David Paulsen of BYU arguing that the earliest Christians held anthropomorphic views of God, later displaced by Greek philosophical categories. On Adam-God, FAIR holds that Young's remarks were poorly recorded, speculative or misunderstood, that they were never canonized, and that the church's rejection shows the self-correcting authority of living prophets rather than prophetic failure.
god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.rationale: Every element is documented from canonized or currently published sources. D&C 130:22 is canon, and the 'Becoming Like God' essay confirms that the church still teaches the exalted-man doctrine. The FAIR reading of John 4:24 has some force in isolation. But the conflict rests on the convergence of texts. A God who 'was once as we are now' cannot be 'from everlasting to everlasting' God, or unchanging as Malachi 3:6 says. A God who progressed inside an eternal framework of matter and law is not the Bible's absolute Creator of all that exists. The Adam-God episode is independently devastating to the self-correction frame. Young taught it explicitly, repeatedly, over 25 years, including inside the temple. Kimball's 1976 denunciation means one prophet formally branded another prophet's pulpit teaching about the identity of God 'false doctrine.'

different-jesus-hinckley-1998.claim: Asked whether Latter-day Saints believe in 'the traditional Christ,' church president Gordon B. Hinckley said in 1998: 'No, I don't. The traditional Christ of whom they speak is not the Christ of whom I speak. For the Christ of whom I speak has been revealed in this the Dispensation of the Fulness of Times.' It is in the Church News of 20 June 1998. That is the sitting prophet conceding, in his own words, the substance of the evangelical claim. The Latter-day Saint Christ — firstborn spirit child, elder brother of Lucifer and of humanity, one of three separate Gods — differs from the Christ of historic Christianity. Paul warns against those who preach 'another Jesus, whom we have not preached' with 'another gospel' (2 Corinthians 11:3-4; Galatians 1:6-9; cf. Matthew 24:23-24, 1 John 4:1-3). The church's essay 'Are Mormons Christian?' responds not by claiming doctrinal agreement but by contesting the definition of 'Christian.'
different-jesus-hinckley-1998.response: FAIR argues the quote is authentic but misused. In context Hinckley was distinguishing the Latter-day Saint Christ from the traditional creedal Christ — the immaterial, incomprehensible being of Nicaea and Chalcedon — not from the Jesus of the New Testament, whom Latter-day Saints insist they worship as divine Son of God, Saviour and Redeemer. 'The Living Christ' of 2000 says exactly that. The 'Are Mormons Christian?' essay adds that the earliest Christians' view of God 'changed dramatically over the course of centuries' under Greek philosophy, so fidelity to fourth-century creeds cannot be the test of who follows Jesus. Latter-day Saints claim restored Christianity, not reformed Christianity. On 2 Corinthians 11:4 they note that Paul's target was a different gospel message, not a doctrinal exam on metaphysics.
different-jesus-hinckley-1998.rationale: The quotation is authentic, verified in the church's own Church News, and Hinckley plainly affirms a real difference. That much is unrefuted, and the difference is substantiated independently by the christology entries. But the inference this entry tests — that the statement is an admission of 'another Jesus' in Paul's sense — is genuinely contested. FAIR's contextual point has real merit. 'Traditional Christ' most naturally refers to the creedal formulation, and Latter-day Saint materials consistently identify their Christ with the New Testament Jesus: the same person, a different metaphysics. Whether that counts as another Jesus should be argued from the doctrinal entries, not settled by this quote alone.

premortal-spirit-children.claim: Latter-day Saint doctrine teaches that every human lived before birth as a literal spirit child begotten by Heavenly Parents. The Gospel Topics essay 'Mother in Heaven' says that 'all human beings, male and female, are beloved spirit children of heavenly parents.' A First Presidency statement of 1909, quoted in Gospel Principles chapter 2, says that man as a spirit 'was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father.' Abraham 3:22-23 describes premortal 'intelligences that were organized before the world was'; see also D&C 93:29 and Moses 3:5. The Bible teaches the reverse order and origin. 'That was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual' (1 Corinthians 15:46-47). The LORD 'formeth the spirit of man within him' (Zechariah 12:1). And man became a living soul when God breathed into formed dust (Genesis 2:7; cf. Isaiah 44:24).
premortal-spirit-children.response: FAIR assembles a biblical case for premortality. God knew Jeremiah 'before I formed thee in the belly' (Jeremiah 1:5). The 'sons of God shouted for joy' at earth's founding (Job 38:4-7). At death 'the spirit shall return unto God who gave it' (Ecclesiastes 12:7), and 'return' implies prior residence. God is 'the Father of spirits' (Hebrews 12:9). And the disciples' question about the man born blind (John 9:2) presupposes possible premortal agency. FAIR adds that the preexistence of souls was a live view in early Christianity, held by Origen, before being condemned in the sixth century. On 1 Corinthians 15:46 they respond that Paul's subject is resurrection bodies, not the origin of spirits.
premortal-spirit-children.rationale: The doctrine is precisely documented from current official sources, and the core conflict stands. No biblical text teaches that human spirits were begotten by Heavenly Parents before the world, and Zechariah 12:1 locates the forming of man's spirit 'within him.' The proof-texts dissolve on context. Jeremiah 1:5 is election and foreknowledge language, as at Romans 8:29. Job 38:7's 'sons of God' are angels, and God's point to Job is that Job was not there. Ecclesiastes 12:7's 'return' parallels dust returning to earth. FAIR is right that 1 Corinthians 15:46 concerns the order of resurrection bodies, so that counter-text is weaker. And Origen shows that soul-preexistence was thinkable early, though his version — with no Heavenly Mother and no spirit birth — is not this doctrine. The distinctive claim, literal celestial procreation of human spirits, remains without any biblical support.

trinity-vs-godhead.claim: Official Latter-day Saint doctrine holds that the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are 'three separate beings,' with the Father and Son having tangible bodies, who are 'one in purpose' but not one Being (Gospel Topics: 'Godhead'; D&C 130:22). Joseph Smith's First Vision account has God declaring all existing creeds 'an abomination in his sight' (Joseph Smith—History 1:19), and the Book of Abraham narrates creation by 'the Gods' (Abraham 4:1). Smith preached a plurality of gods explicitly in the Sermon in the Grove of June 1844. The Bible's monotheism is exclusive and about being, not merely about purpose. 'The LORD our God is one LORD' (Deuteronomy 6:4). 'I am the LORD that maketh all things; that stretcheth forth the heavens alone; that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself' (Isaiah 44:24) — no council of gods at creation. 'There is none other God but one' (1 Corinthians 8:4-6; cf. Isaiah 43:10, 45:5-6). Notably, the Book of Mormon itself reads monotheistically: Alma 11:28-29 asks 'Is there more than one God?' and answers no. So does 2 Nephi 31:21.
trinity-vs-godhead.response: The strongest case runs on four fronts. First, Jesus prays that believers 'may be one, even as we are one' (John 17:20-23). Believers cannot merge into one substance, so the oneness of Father and Son in the same sentence is most naturally relational — exactly the 'one in purpose' reading. Second, Jesus is visibly distinct from the Father throughout the New Testament: at his baptism, in Gethsemane, and in Stephen's vision at Acts 7:55-56. 1 Corinthians 8:6 distinguishes 'one God, the Father' from 'one Lord, Jesus Christ.' Third, respected Christian philosophers — Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, William Lane Craig — model the Trinity as three centres of consciousness united in essence and will, and BYU scholars argue that this lands close to Joseph Smith's Godhead. The disagreement, they say, is with post-biblical Greek metaphysics, not with the Bible. Fourth, Hebrew scholarship on the divine council in Psalm 82 shows plural elohim language native to the Old Testament.
trinity-vs-godhead.rationale: The doctrine is accurately documented, and a real conflict exists. But the steelman has genuine merit at exactly the point this entry tests. The relational reading of John 17 is exegetically defensible, and social trinitarianism is a live position within Christian philosophy. The conflict becomes sharp only where this doctrine exceeds it. Social trinitarians still affirm one necessarily existent, uncreated divine essence. Latter-day Saint theology has three independent beings, two of them embodied, at least one of whom attained divinity, with exaltation extending godhood to others. Isaiah 44:24's 'alone… by myself' and Isaiah 43:10 exclude that plurality. Note the internal tension too: the Book of Mormon reads monotheistically in Alma 11, against Smith's later Nauvoo theology. Graded contested because the John 17 argument succeeds on its own ground; the decisive conflict lives in Isaiah and in the christology entries.

adam-god-doctrine.claim: On 9 April 1852, Brigham Young taught in general conference that Adam 'is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do' (Journal of Discourses 1:50-51). He repeated the teaching for over two decades, declaring in 1873 that 'Adam is my father' was doctrine God had revealed to him. In 1877 he had it incorporated into the temple lecture at the veil in the St George Temple, as recorded in L. John Nuttall's journal for 7 February 1877. The teaching contradicts Genesis, where Adam is a creature formed by God (Genesis 2:7), the Bible's insistence that God is not a man (Hosea 11:9; Isaiah 43:10; 1 Corinthians 15:45), and canonized Latter-day Saint scripture itself, which identifies Adam as the archangel Michael, subordinate to God (D&C 27:11; 107:53-55). In 1976, President Spencer W. Kimball told general conference: 'the Adam-God theory… We denounce that theory and hope that everyone will be cautioned against this and other kinds of false doctrine.' Either a prophet taught false doctrine over the pulpit and in the temple for 25 years, or the church now denounces true doctrine.
adam-god-doctrine.response: FAIR argues that Young's sermons survive in imperfect transcriptions, that he elsewhere taught things inconsistent with a strong Adam-God reading, and that the teaching was never canonized by common consent. On that account it was a prophet's personal theological speculation, not church doctrine. Kimball's 1976 denunciation is presented as the system working. The living church self-corrects, and doctrine is defined by canonized scripture and the united voice of the First Presidency, not by every pulpit statement of a past president.
adam-god-doctrine.rationale: Kimball's 1976 denunciation concedes the substance. Something Young taught as doctrine is now officially 'false doctrine.' The misreporting defense fails against multiple independent records: the Journal of Discourses, Young's own 1873 reaffirmation, Wilford Woodruff's journal, and the St George temple lecture minutes. The remaining move — that it was never canonized — rescues the church's doctrinal process only by conceding the evangelistic point. A president of the church, speaking as prophet, taught for 25 years, including inside the temple, something the church now denounces. That collapses 'the prophet will never lead the church astray' as a working guarantee.

lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.claim: 'As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.' Lorenzo Snow wrote the couplet in 1840. Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse of 1844 ratified it, and prophets and manuals have taught it ever since; the Teachings of the Presidents: Lorenzo Snow manual features it, and D&C 130:22 stands behind it. Yet when Richard Ostling of Time asked President Hinckley in 1997 whether God the Father was once a man, Hinckley answered: 'I don't know that we teach it. I don't know that we emphasize it… I understand the philosophical background behind it, but I don't know a lot about it.' He gave a similar deflection to the San Francisco Chronicle, calling it 'more of a couplet than anything else.' The 2014 essay 'Becoming Like God' robustly affirms the second half, human deification, while treating the first half — God's past as a man — with studied vagueness. So which is it: doctrine, speculation, or retired? The distinct issue here is institutional candour. What is taught inside is minimized outside. Psalm 90:2, Isaiah 43:10, Numbers 23:19 and Malachi 3:6 are the texts at issue.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.response: Apologists say Hinckley was answering narrowly. The church does not emphasize or elaborate the doctrine because little has been revealed about it, and he was not denying it. Hinckley told the next General Conference that news reports were 'incomplete.' The 'Becoming Like God' essay affirms that humans can become like God, while noting that scripture says little about God's past.
lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.rationale: Grade this on the candour gap, not on the doctrine itself; the doctrine is the exalted-man case, covered separately. The same church that publishes a prophet's manual featuring the couplet had its sitting prophet tell national media 'I don't know that we teach it.' Either the prophet did not know his own doctrine, or he was managing its public image. Both are problems for a church claiming prophetic clarity. Ronald Huggins, writing in the Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society in 2006, traces the couplet's canonical-grade usage in church curricula, so 'we don't really teach it' is documentedly false. This is conversationally strong. Most members have sung 'If You Could Hie to Kolob' and learned the couplet, and showing them Hinckley's answer lands.

facsimile-1-lion-couch.claim: Joseph Smith published Facsimile 1 as Abraham 'fastened upon an altar,' with 'the idolatrous priest of Elkenah attempting to offer up Abraham as a sacrifice' (Facsimile 1 Explanation, figures 2 and 3; cf. Abraham 1:12-15). Egyptology identifies the original as a standard funerary lion-couch vignette: the jackal-headed god Anubis attending the deceased Osiris-Hor. It survives as Papyrus Joseph Smith I. That is part of the Book of Breathings made for the Theban priest Hor, in the Ptolemaic era, around the second or first century BC. That is more than 1,500 years after Abraham. The papyrus has a lacuna, a missing section, exactly where the priest's head and alleged knife appear in the 1842 published version. The woodcut restoration shows a bald human head and a drawn knife. Robert Ritner and others note ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder, indicating a jackal-headed Anubis, and no parallel vignette shows a knife. Smith's other identifications do not match any accepted Egyptological reading either: the bird as 'Angel of the Lord,' the canopic jars as idolatrous gods of foreign nations, the crocodile as 'idolatrous god of Pharaoh.'
facsimile-1-lion-couch.response: John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue four things. First, the lacuna means nobody knows what the original showed. Some apologists hold that the papyrus was already damaged in 1835, and that a knife and a human head could have stood there. They note the vignette is unusual among lion-couch scenes, since the figure on the couch appears alive, clothed, and with both hands possibly raised. Second, there is Egyptian evidence for the ritual slaying of enemies in temple contexts, so a 'sacrifice' reading is not absurd. Third, on the Semitic-adaptation theory, ancient Jews in Egypt demonstrably reused and reinterpreted Egyptian iconography, so the vignette could have illustrated an Abraham text regardless of its funerary origin. Fourth, on the catalyst theory the Book of Abraham is a revealed text for which the papyri were merely a prompt, making the explanations inspired commentary rather than Egyptological translation.
facsimile-1-lion-couch.rationale: Unlike Facsimiles 2 and 3, this one contains a genuine evidentiary gap. The lacuna covers precisely the disputed elements, so the restoration argument runs on parallels and ink traces rather than on a surviving original. The scholarly consensus is far better supported: Anubis in a routine embalming and resurrection scene from Hor's Breathing Permit, with headdress traces, hundreds of parallel vignettes, and zero parallels showing a knife. The church's own essay concedes that Egyptologists' readings differ from Smith's. But because apologists dispute what filled the lacuna rather than the Egyptology itself, and the vignette does have unusual features, this figure-level claim is scored contested rather than unrefuted. Note that the surrounding identifications — the canopic jars as foreign gods, the crocodile as Pharaoh's god — find no Egyptological support at all.

facsimile-2-hypocephalus.claim: Facsimile 2 is a hypocephalus: a funerary amulet placed under a mummy's head, from Book of the Dead spell 162, made for a man named Sheshonq. It is a well-understood class of object, meant to keep the deceased warm and to aid resurrection. Joseph Smith's explanations instead present it as cosmology. Figure 1 is 'Kolob, signifying the first creation, nearest to the celestial, or the residence of God.' Figure 5 is the sun receiving light 'through the medium of Kae-e-vanrash.' Abraham 3:2-4 and 3:9 go with them. Most starkly, there is figure 7. Egyptologists uniformly identify it as Min, an ithyphallic fertility god, shown seated with an erect phallus and upraised flail, approached by a serpent. Smith labelled it 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing through the heavens the grand Key-words of the Priesthood; as, also, the sign of the Holy Ghost unto Abraham, in the form of a dove.' Even the Latter-day Saint scholar Michael Rhodes's translation of the rim and panels yields standard funerary formulae for Sheshonq, not Abrahamic cosmology. Portions of the original were missing and were filled in for the 1842 publication with characters copied from other papyri, including lines from the Hor Book of Breathings.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.response: Latter-day Saint scholarship concedes that figure 7 depicts a form of Min. Rhodes, Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central all grant it. They then argue three things. First, Min was for Egyptians a supreme creator god. He stood for the power that makes life. So 'God sitting upon his throne' may catch the figure's role in Egyptian religion, even if the image shocks a modern reader. Second, hypocephali are esoteric objects, encoding cosmic geography and rebirth. A cosmological reading is therefore not alien to the genre. A few of Smith's identifications are argued to land near Egyptian ideas — figure 1 linked to the creative force at the centre, and figure 4 as expanse or firmament. Third, under the Semitic-adaptation and catalyst frameworks, the explanations were never meant as decipherment. They were inspired repurposing, in the way Egyptian Jews reused pagan imagery.
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.rationale: There is no dispute about what figure 7 is. Apologetic sources themselves identify it as ithyphallic Min. The dispute is only whether 'God sitting upon his throne, revealing the grand Key-words of the Priesthood… the sign of the Holy Ghost… in the form of a dove' can be rescued as a functional-equivalence reading of a pagan fertility figure approached by a serpent. No Egyptologist reads the hypocephalus as teaching Kolob, priesthood key-words, or the Holy Ghost. Rhodes's own faithful translation of the object's actual text yields conventional funerary petitions for Sheshonq. The steelman does not counter the translation evidence. It relocates Smith's explanations outside translation entirely, which concedes the empirical point while contesting its theological weight. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 set the test. Smith claimed to translate by the gift and power of God. The specific, checkable claims fail checking, and no counter-translation has answered them.

facsimile-3-presentation.claim: Facsimile 3 is a standard presentation vignette from the Book of Breathings of the priest Hor. The deceased Hor, led by Maat and Anubis, is presented before the enthroned Osiris, with Isis behind him. Unlike Facsimile 1, the hieroglyphic captions beside each figure survive in the published woodcut and name the figures, and Egyptologists can read them. Robert Ritner's translations run as follows. Figure 2, which Smith labelled 'King Pharaoh, whose name is given in the characters above his head,' is captioned 'Isis the great, the god's mother' — a goddess. Figure 4, which Smith called 'Prince of Pharaoh, King of Egypt, as written above the hand,' is 'Maat, mistress of the gods' — also a goddess. Figure 1, Smith's 'Abraham sitting upon Pharaoh's throne,' is the god Osiris. Figure 5, Smith's 'Shulem, one of the king's principal waiters,' is captioned 'The Osiris Hor, justified forever' — the papyrus owner himself. Figure 6, Smith's 'Olimlah, a slave belonging to the prince,' is the god Anubis. Smith thus rendered two female goddesses as male royalty, and claimed their names were given in the characters above — characters that, once read, name Isis and Maat. Earlier Egyptologists shown the facsimiles reached the same conclusions independently: Théodule Devéria in 1860, and the 1912 panel that included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted.
facsimile-3-presentation.response: The strongest apologetic — Gee, Muhlestein, and Pearl of Great Price Central — does not offer a rival translation of the captions. It accepts the Egyptological readings and argues for reidentification. First, in Egyptian theology Pharaoh was understood as the earthly embodiment of Osiris, and Isis could be ritually identified with the throne, and even with the king, so 'Isis as Pharaoh' has attested conceptual precedent. Second, ancient Semitic peoples demonstrably adapted Egyptian vignettes for their own figures — Jewish reuse of Egyptian iconography, and Abraham appearing in later Egyptian magical texts — so an ancient Jewish redactor could have relabelled this scene as an Abraham-at-court illustration. Third, presentation scenes involve dressing figures in others' iconography, so gender-crossing identifications are not unknown in Egyptian ritual texts. Fourth, some caption glyphs, notably the Isis name group, are poorly copied in the woodcut, which complicates certainty about what stood on the original.
facsimile-3-presentation.rationale: This is the hardest facsimile case for the Latter-day Saint position. Smith explicitly staked his labels on the characters themselves — 'whose name is given in the characters above his head' — and those characters, now readable, name Isis and Maat, not any Pharaoh or prince. They name the papyrus owner Hor where Smith saw 'Shulem the waiter.' No apologetic source produces a counter-translation. The Semitic-adaptation steelman concedes the Egyptology and posits an undocumented ancient relabelling, for which no direct evidence exists on this papyrus. The church's own essay concedes that Egyptologists' interpretations do not match Smith's, but stops short of conceding error, so the verdict is unrefuted rather than admitted. As a directly checkable translation claim made in the name of the gift and power of God, it fails the test of 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and Deuteronomy 18 on the evidence as it stands.

egyptian-alphabet-grammar.claim: Alongside the Book of Abraham translation, Joseph Smith's circle produced the Kirtland Egyptian Papers. Among them is a bound 'Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language' from 1835, in the hands of W. W. Phelps and Warren Parrish, published in full by the Joseph Smith Papers. Joseph's own journal records him 'studying the Egyptian language,' and records that the group was 'engaged in translating an alphabet to the Book of Abraham, and arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language.' The system assigns single Egyptian characters paragraph-long English meanings that multiply through five 'degrees' — a scheme Egyptologists uniformly reject as bearing no relation to actual Egyptian. Three Book of Abraham manuscripts place characters copied sequentially from the recovered Hor Book of Breathings in the margins, beside the English text. Unlike the gold plates, here the working papers of a Joseph Smith translation project survive, and they show a method that was not translation. Abraham 1:1-3 is the text at issue, and Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and Jeremiah 23:16 the tests applied.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar.response: Apologists — Gee, Muhlestein, and Pearl of Great Price Central — argue that the direction of dependence is reversed. The Egyptian-language documents were the scribes' after-the-fact attempt to reverse-engineer Egyptian using the already-revealed English text. It was an intellectual exercise Joseph tolerated but did not author. Most pages are in scribes' handwriting. The Grammar was never published or canonized. And they argue that textual evidence shows the Abraham text preceding the Alphabet entries. On this view the Kirtland Egyptian Papers tell us about 1835 curiosity regarding Egyptian, not about how the Book of Abraham was produced.
egyptian-alphabet-grammar.rationale: The narrow question is which came first: the English text, or the Alphabet documents. That is genuinely debated. Joseph Smith Papers editors call the documents intertwined, and scholars on both sides make textual arguments. So the strongest critical framing — that the Grammar was the engine of translation — stays contested. But the escape is expensive. Joseph's own journal says he was arranging the grammar. Either way, his circle produced an 'Egyptian' system under his eye, and it is nonsense. Set beside the papyri mismatch, covered separately, this backs up the case rather than making it alone. Hence medium severity, and a cautious contested grade.

endowment-masonic-origins.claim: Joseph Smith was initiated into Freemasonry in Nauvoo on 15 and 16 March 1842. He rose to Master Mason in a single day. Seven weeks later, on 4 May 1842, he introduced the temple endowment. The first nine men to receive it were all Masons. The church's own history essay acknowledges these facts. The two rites shared documented elements. Tokens, which are grips. Signs. Key words. Ritual penalties miming throat-cutting and disembowelment. The five points of fellowship. And the compass-and-square symbols. The penalty oaths and the five points were removed from the ceremony in April 1990. Critics contrast the covenant of non-disclosure with Jesus's 'in secret have I said nothing' (John 18:20; cf. Matthew 10:26-27, Ephesians 5:11-13). They argue that a restored ancient ordinance should not track eighteenth-century Masonic ritual in datable detail.
endowment-masonic-origins.response: The church and FAIR concede the parallels, but separate form from substance. Masonry served as a 'catalyst for revelation.' It gave Joseph a familiar ritual vocabulary in which to teach covenants that were genuinely revealed. The endowment's content has no Masonic counterpart: creation, fall, redemption, and covenants of consecration. Unlike Masonry, it was given to women and to 'even the weakest of the Saints.' FAIR argues that the ritual is the vehicle, not the endowment itself. So revising it, as in 1990 and 2019, is continuing revelation rather than damage control. And the temple is 'sacred, not secret.' Its teachings are published. Only certain signs and tokens are withheld by covenant, much as Jesus held some things back from public teaching (Mark 4:34; John 16:12).
endowment-masonic-origins.rationale: The factual claim is documented, and effectively conceded by the church's own essay. Masonic initiation weeks before the endowment. Borrowed ritual elements. The later removal of the penalty oaths and the five points. The 'catalyst' framing interprets those facts rather than rebutting them. And the older apologetic, which argued ancient origins — the endowment as preserved Solomonic ritual — has been quietly abandoned.

avoid-worship-joseph-smith.claim: The popular version says Mormons worship Joseph Smith, and even sing hymns of praise to him — Hymn 27, 'Praise to the Man,' and D&C 135:3. The texts cited against it are Exodus 20:3-5 and Acts 10:25-26.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.response: That is false as stated. Latter-day Saints worship God the Father and Jesus Christ, not Smith. The church explicitly denies worshipping him, and members experience the accusation as an obvious misrepresentation. 'Praise to the Man' is veneration of a founder, with admittedly extravagant language — 'mingling with Gods' — but it is not liturgical worship.
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.rationale: Opening with 'you worship Joseph Smith' is factually wrong, instantly correctable, and marks you as someone who never met a Latter-day Saint. Here is what is true and useful instead. Everything distinctive in Mormonism rests on Smith's claims. Joseph Fielding Smith wrote that 'Mormonism, as it is called, must stand or fall on the story of Joseph Smith' (Doctrines of Salvation 1:188). Say that. 'I know you worship Christ — but every distinctive doctrine depends on whether Joseph told the truth. Can we test that?' It is a door the member's own leaders opened.

avoid-coca-cola-ownership.claim: The popular version says the church secretly owns Coca-Cola, or Pepsi — banning caffeine while profiting from it. D&C 89, the Word of Wisdom, is the supposed irony hook.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership.response: It is an urban legend, and flatly false. Snopes traces it to the appeal of a delicious irony. No ownership stake has ever existed. Ensign Peak's post-settlement 13F disclosures list no Coca-Cola, no PepsiCo and no Keurig Dr Pepper holdings. The legend also rests on a second error, since the church never banned caffeine.
avoid-coca-cola-ownership.rationale: Repeating a legend that Snopes has debunked hands the member a free win, and taints everything else you say. The documented finance story is far stronger than the legend. Ensign Peak's concealed reserve of more than $100 billion, and the 2023 SEC settlement, are already on this site as admitted and adjudicated fact. If church money is the topic, go there. 'The SEC fined your church for hiding $32 billion behind shell companies' needs no urban legend's help.

avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.claim: The popular version says Mormons wear 'magic underwear' that protects them from harm. The texts that bear on how to speak are 1 Peter 3:15-16 and Colossians 4:6.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.response: The garments are real and the practice is documented — see the temple-garments case. But 'magic underwear' is mockery, not argument. The church's 2014 video 'Sacred Temple Clothing' pre-empts exactly this line. It compares garments to the nun's habit, the prayer shawl and the monk's robe, and calls the phrase 'inaccurate and offensive.' Folk beliefs about physical protection do exist among members, but they are not official doctrine.
avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.rationale: Mocking someone's underclothing makes the Christian the aggressor. It triggers the persecution frame the church has already built a video around, and it forfeits the substantive point. The garments case worth making is about enforcement, not fabric. Wearing is monitored through temple-recommend interview questions, and until recently women's garment norms were policed in detail. That is a question about religious control, and it survives being said respectfully. Ask, do not jeer: 'How did it feel to have an interview cover your underwear?'

avoid-white-horse-prophecy.claim: The popular version says Latter-day Saint doctrine holds that a Mormon will ride in to save the Constitution when it hangs by a thread. That is the White Horse Prophecy. It adds that Mormon politicians believe they are the one.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy.response: The church officially repudiated it in 2010. Its statement says the story is 'based on accounts that have not been substantiated by historical research and is not embraced as Church doctrine.' The full White Horse text is a secondhand recollection from 1902, of dubious provenance. There is a kernel to keep, though. The narrower motif — that the Constitution will hang by a thread and the elders will save it — is genuinely and repeatedly attested in leaders' teaching. Brigham Young and John Taylor taught it, and modern leaders such as Ezra Taft Benson invoked it.
avoid-white-horse-prophecy.rationale: Cite the White Horse document as doctrine and the member quotes the 2010 repudiation back at you, and the conversation is over. The defensible move is the kernel. The hang-by-a-thread teaching came from prophets' own mouths in documented sermons, including Journal of Discourses 7:15. That raises the same question with sources the church cannot disown as folklore. Use the thread quotes. Never lead with 'White Horse.'

avoid-caffeine-ban.claim: The popular version says Mormons are not allowed caffeine — no Coke, no Dr Pepper. It hangs on D&C 89:9, 'hot drinks are not for the body or belly.' Mark 7:18-19 and Colossians 2:20-23 are the texts critics reach for.
avoid-caffeine-ban.response: That is false. The Word of Wisdom's 'hot drinks' has been officially interpreted as coffee and tea only. The church stated in 2012 that 'the Church does not prohibit the use of caffeine,' and BYU has sold caffeinated soda since 2017. Many faithful members drink Coke, and caffeine appears nowhere in a temple-recommend interview.
avoid-caffeine-ban.rationale: Getting this wrong signals that you know Mormonism from playground rumour. The incoherence you were reaching for is sharper when stated accurately, and it is already on this site in the Word of Wisdom case. Iced coffee is a temple-worthiness bar while a quad-shot energy drink is fine. The canonized text calls itself 'not by commandment or constraint' at D&C 89:2, yet became a salvation-gating test decades later. And 'hot drinks' meaning exactly coffee and tea is itself a later interpretation. Ask why the line falls where it does. Do not misstate where the line is.

avoid-own-planet.claim: The popular version says Mormons believe that if they are good enough, each of them gets their own planet when they die. The texts at issue are D&C 132:19-20 and Moses 1:33, against Isaiah 43:10 and Isaiah 44:6-8.
avoid-own-planet.response: The church's 2014 essay pre-loaded the rebuttal. Exaltation, it says, is 'reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets,' and a church FAQ answers the planet question with 'No.' Say 'own planet' and the member hands you the essay. The kernel, though, is strong and church-affirmed. Exaltation means becoming gods — D&C 132:20 says 'then shall they be gods' — with eternal increase and participation in creation. Past leaders taught it in exactly cosmic terms: Lorenzo Snow, Brigham Young, and Spencer W. Kimball's 'we shall create worlds.'
avoid-own-planet.rationale: This is the rare avoid-entry where the underlying doctrine is fully conceded. The error is purely in the packaging. 'Own planet' is South Park vocabulary that the church has explicitly framed as caricature, so using it triggers the scripted deflection and skips the real conversation. Use the member's own words instead. 'Your scripture says the exalted shall be gods — D&C 132:20. Isaiah says before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. Can both be true?' The exaltation case on this site carries the full argument.

avoid-1826-convicted-conman.claim: The popular version says Joseph Smith was a convicted con man — that a court convicted him of fraud in 1826, right before he found the plates.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman.response: That is overclaimed. The 1826 Bainbridge proceeding was real. Smith, aged 20, was charged as a 'disorderly person' over paid 'glass looking,' and Justice Neely's own fee bill labels him 'The Glass Looker.' But it was likely a preliminary examination. The surviving records are fragmentary and contradictory: the Pearsall account says 'guilty,' while the fee bill and mittimus evidence point the other way. Scholars dispute the outcome, from Gordon Madsen, who reads an acquittal or discharge, to Dan Vogel and Wesley Walters. 'Convicted of fraud' states as fact what the documents cannot establish.
avoid-1826-convicted-conman.rationale: Say 'convicted' and the apologist wins the exchange on the record's ambiguity — and the ambiguity is genuine, not spin. Here is the core that needs no conviction. By the church's own Gospel Topics admission, and by Richard Bushman in Rough Stone Rolling, Smith was a paid treasure-seer who hunted buried valuables by staring at a stone in his hat. It was the same stone, in the same hat, that he then used to produce the Book of Mormon. The 1826 court documents corroborate that occupation regardless of the verdict. Use it as corroboration, not as your lead. Lead with the church-admitted seer-stone facts, covered in the translation case, and let the 1826 record confirm the timeline.

prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.claim: Latter-day Saint prophets have taught, from prophetic platforms, doctrines the church later abandoned or disavowed. Brigham Young affirmed that the moon and the sun are inhabited (Journal of Discourses 13:271, 1870), and taught Adam-God in general conference, later denounced as 'false doctrine' by Spencer W. Kimball. Bruce R. McConkie's 'Mormon Doctrine' of 1958 required over 1,000 corrections identified by apostolic review, yet sold for decades before being pulled in 2010. Meanwhile Wilford Woodruff's declaration is printed with Official Declaration 1 in the canon: 'The Lord will never permit me or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray.' That creates an unfalsifiable loop. Whatever prophets teach is prophetic until it isn't, and the errors retroactively become 'opinion.' Deuteronomy 18:21-22, Matthew 7:15-20 and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 are the tests applied.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.response: The church expressly teaches that prophets are fallible men. Joseph Smith said that 'a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such,' and not every sermon is revelation. Young's musing about the moon and sun was explicit speculation — 'I rather think it is' — and it was consistent with mainstream nineteenth-century science, since William Herschel believed the sun inhabited. It was never canonized or made a test of faith. Mormon Doctrine was a private book McConkie published without authorization, so its correction and eventual withdrawal show the system self-correcting rather than failing. And Woodruff's statement, in context, addressed the specific fear that the Manifesto was apostasy. It promises that God would remove a president who attempted to lead the church fundamentally astray, not that presidents never err.
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.rationale: The quotes are authentic and verifiable. But the claim's force depends on whether these were held as prophetic, and the apologetic case has real substance. Young flagged the moon and sun comment as opinion, and McConkie's book was never official. Adam-God is the critics' strongest example, since it was taught in conference as doctrine and later disavowed, and it keeps the tension live. The unfalsifiability critique of Woodruff's dictum is a fair philosophical point. As a factual claim of failed prophecy, this is genuinely contested territory.

kirtland-safety-society.claim: In November 1836 Joseph Smith co-founded the Kirtland Safety Society bank. When the Ohio legislature denied a charter, it reorganized in January 1837 as the 'Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company' and issued notes anyway. On 6 January 1837, Wilford Woodruff recorded in his journal that Smith declared he had 'receieved that morning the word of the Lord upon the subject of the Kirtland Safety Society' — not only 'the voice of the spirit… but even an audaible voice' — and that if the commandments were heeded 'all would be well.' Warren Parrish, an officer of the bank who later left the church, claimed Smith prophesied it would 'like Aaron's rod… swallow up all other banks… and survive when all others should be laid in ruins.' The bank was massively undercapitalized, and its notes lost most of their value within weeks. On 24 October 1837, Smith and Sidney Rigdon were each fined $1,000 plus costs for illegal banking, in Rounds qui tam v. Smith, under Ohio's 1816 statute. Smith fled Kirtland on the night of 12 January 1838. Historians estimate that 200 to 300 members left the church in the fallout — roughly 10 to 15% of Kirtland membership, including about a third of the general leadership. Heber C. Kimball later said that at the time, for every member who stood by Joseph Smith as prophet, 'there were twenty who did not.'
kirtland-safety-society.response: FAIR and church historians argue five things. The 1830s were the era of unregulated 'wildcat' banking, and hundreds of banks, many of them chartered, failed in the national Panic of 1837, so the collapse reflects the economy rather than fraud. The charter denial owed to Ohio legislative politics, since hard-money Democrats denied nearly all new charters that session, and anti-Mormon sentiment may have contributed; operating as a joint-stock 'anti-banking' company followed legal counsel's advice under genuinely unsettled law. Joseph Smith invested more of his own money than almost anyone and lost heavily, which is the opposite of a fraudster's profile. He resigned in June 1837 and publicly warned the Saints against the notes before the worst of the collapse. And Woodruff's journal does not record the content of the claimed revelation, while the grandiose 'swallow up all banks' prophecy comes only from Warren Parrish, by then a hostile ex-member with his own alleged role in the failure.
kirtland-safety-society.rationale: The load-bearing facts are conceded in the church's own publications. The Joseph Smith Papers and the Church History Topics essay acknowledge the charter denial, the decision to operate anyway, the October 1837 fines for illegal banking, Smith's flight to Missouri, and that leaders bore responsibility for failing to anticipate problems. The revelation claim rests not on hostile sources but on the faithful, contemporaneous Woodruff journal, published by the church-affiliated Woodruff Papers Project. Smith attached 'the word of the Lord' and an 'audible voice' to an enterprise that failed within months, was ruled illegal, and triggered the largest apostasy of his lifetime. The steelman genuinely mitigates intent — fraud is not established, the Panic of 1837 was real, and Parrish's version deserves discounting as hostile — but it does not touch the core problem under Deuteronomy 18:21-22. A claimed divine assurance that 'all would be well' was falsified by events. Severity is tempered only in that the revelation's full wording was never recorded, so the strongest prophecy framing depends partly on Parrish.

priesthood-restoration-late-account.claim: The church teaches that John the Baptist restored the Aaronic priesthood in May 1829. See D&C 13 and Joseph Smith—History 1:68-72. Peter, James and John are said to have restored the Melchizedek priesthood soon after. Yet no publication or record describes these angelic ordinations until Oliver Cowdery's account of October 1834, in the Messenger and Advocate. That is five years later. Joseph's 1832 history does not narrate them. The 1833 Book of Commandments revelations contain none of the passages. And the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants added the relevant text retroactively. What is now D&C 27:5-13 grew from a short 1830 revelation into one naming John the Baptist and Peter, James and John. Compare Book of Commandments 28. David Whitmer told interviewers he 'never heard that an Angel had ordained Joseph and Oliver to the Aaronic priesthood' until years after the church was organized in 1830, and William McLellin said the same. Critics conclude that the restoration narrative developed after 1830 and was written back into the founding revelations. Hebrews 7:23-24, 1 Peter 2:9 and Deuteronomy 4:2 are the texts at issue.
priesthood-restoration-late-account.response: FAIR and BYU scholars reply that Joseph's 1832 history does mention receiving 'the holy Priesthood by the ministring of Aangels,' and that an 1829-era revelation, now D&C 27, alludes to authority from heavenly messengers. Joseph and Oliver kept the details private because of intense persecution; Joseph said they were 'forced to keep secret the circumstances of having received the Priesthood.' The 1835 expansions are framed as the prophet clarifying earlier revelations under the same inspiration. And Whitmer's and McLellin's recollections are dismissed as hostile memories recorded four to five decades later.
priesthood-restoration-late-account.rationale: The documented facts favor the critics. The named-angel narrative appears nowhere before 1834, and the 1835 additions are visible in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers. But the apologetic case is not empty. The 1832 history's 'ministring of Aangels' phrase and the persecution-secrecy argument are genuine, if ambiguous, counters, and late hostile recollections deserve discounting. What is beyond dispute is the retroactive textual expansion. What remains arguable is whether it records suppressed events or invents them. That split — solid textual evidence, live alternative explanation — is the definition of contested, though the pattern matches the First Vision's evolving accounts.

book-of-commandments-revisions.claim: Revelations published in 1833 as the direct word of God were materially rewritten for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants. There were hundreds of changes, including substantive additions and reversals, all verifiable in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers scans. Book of Commandments 4:2 says God 'will grant him no other gift' than translating the Book of Mormon; D&C 5:4 rewrites this to 'no other gift until it is finished,' opening the door to Joseph's later revelatory career. Book of Commandments 7 says Oliver Cowdery's gift is 'working with the rod,' the 'rod of nature'; D&C 8:6-9 renames the divining rod 'the gift of Aaron.' Book of Commandments 28, now D&C 27:5-13, grew from a short revelation into eighteen verses naming the priesthood-restoring angels. Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5-6 forbid adding to God's words. A 'thus saith the Lord' text that must be re-engineered years later, to fit the movement's development, looks like an evolving human composition rather than delivered revelation.
book-of-commandments-revisions.response: FAIR argues that Joseph Smith never claimed word-for-word divine dictation. Revelations came as impressions expressed in his own imperfect language, so the prophet who received them had authority to revise, expand and update them as church organization and his understanding grew. Section 20's ecclesiastical additions simply incorporated offices revealed after 1830. The church publishes every version openly through the Joseph Smith Papers, which FAIR presents as the opposite of concealment. And the revised texts were accepted by common consent of the 1835 conference.
book-of-commandments-revisions.rationale: The changes themselves are conceded and published by the church. The Joseph Smith Papers project puts both editions side by side, and FAIR's defense is a justification of the edits rather than a denial of them. That satisfies 'admitted': the church's own publications concede the substance. The remaining dispute is interpretive — whether a prophet may revise God's words — and there the apologetic answer creates its own problem. If revelations are Joseph's fallible paraphrases, subject to later re-engineering, then the weight of any given 'thus saith the Lord' is correspondingly reduced, including D&C 132. Severity is medium because the fact is damaging chiefly in combination with the priesthood-restoration backdating.

zelph-white-lamanite.claim: On 3 June 1834, during Zion's Camp, Joseph Smith's men dug a skeleton with an arrowhead between its ribs from a burial mound near the Illinois River. The site is Naples-Russell Mound 8, a Hopewell-culture site in Pike County, Illinois. According to diaries kept by at least six participants — Wilford Woodruff, Heber C. Kimball, George A. Smith, Levi Hancock, Moses Martin and Reuben McBride — Joseph declared by vision that the bones belonged to 'Zelph,' a 'white Lamanite' warrior-chieftain under 'the great prophet Onandagus,' killed in battle. Several accounts say Onandagus was 'known from the Rocky Mountains to the eastern sea.' The story entered History of the Church 2:79-80. The episode shows Joseph exercising his revelatory gift on a checkable claim — a Hopewell burial unrelated to any Israelite civilization — and locating Book of Mormon peoples in North America, which limited Mesoamerican geography models must explain away. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 is the test applied.
zelph-white-lamanite.response: FAIR, drawing on Kenneth Godfrey's source study, notes that Joseph himself wrote nothing about Zelph. The six diary accounts disagree on key details, such as which battle it was and whether the Rocky Mountains phrase was original. The History of the Church version is a later scribal conflation that hardened a casual campfire comment into formal revelation. And even taken at face value, apologists argue that Zelph could be a late-period Lamanite in the hinterlands, far from the Book of Mormon's core lands, so the story does not fix Book of Mormon geography.
zelph-white-lamanite.rationale: The source-critical objections are real. The accounts genuinely diverge on details, and the canonical History version is a conflation, so the exact content of Joseph's statement is not recoverable with certainty. That keeps this out of 'unrefuted.' But all six independent diaries agree on the core. Joseph claimed a vision identifying a specific skeleton as a white Lamanite under a prophet named Onandagus. That core is either a false revelatory claim about a Hopewell burial, or it must be diluted to speculation — the same unfalsifiability move seen elsewhere. Contested on the details, damaging on the pattern, and medium severity.

bom-geography-retreat.claim: For over a century the church taught a hemispheric Book of Mormon. Canonized revelations identify North American Indians as Lamanites (D&C 28:8; 32:2; 54:8). Joseph Smith endorsed ruins in Central America as Nephite, in the Times and Seasons of 1842. He endorsed North American sites too — the 'plains of the Nephites,' and Zelph. The New York hill where he got the plates was officially the Cumorah of the final battles (Mormon 6:6). Joseph Fielding Smith warned that a two-Cumorah theory would make members 'confused and disturbed in their faith.' Marion Romney affirmed the New York Cumorah in general conference in 1975. Under pressure from digging and from DNA, scholars retreated to limited-geography models. Two rival camps now argue. The Mesoamerican one, at FAIR and Scripture Central. The Heartland one, at Rod Meldrum's FIRM Foundation. Each publishes detailed refutations of the other. In 2019 the church's Gospel Topics statement said it 'does not take a position on the specific geographic locations,' and asked members not to teach any geography in church settings. No model reconciles the text, the founders' statements and the evidence.
bom-geography-retreat.response: Apologists respond that the text itself never names a modern location. They add that internal travel distances actually require a limited geography. So the hemispheric model was a cultural assumption that early members layered onto the text, Joseph among them, speaking as a man. It was not revelation. Scripture Central argues that a Mesoamerican setting satisfies dozens of textual criteria: writing systems, cities, warfare, demographics. And the church's official neutrality is fitting humility on a question scripture leaves open. They compare it to unresolved questions in biblical geography.
bom-geography-retreat.rationale: The retreat itself is documented in the church's own statement. The defense that the text never specifies a place fails against canonized text. The Doctrine and Covenants is scripture, not speculation, and it names specific North American tribes as Lamanites. Prophets taught the New York Cumorah as doctrine. The strongest evidence that no answer works is the apologists themselves. FAIR and Scripture Central publish refutations of the Heartland model. Their arguments — anachronism, distance, archaeology — mirror the critics' case against Mesoamerica. The Heartland side returns the favour. When every proposed location is convincingly refuted by fellow believers, the claim has become unfalsifiable by relocation. Medium severity, because it is a meta-argument that leans on the archaeology and DNA entries.

holocaust-proxy-baptisms.claim: Latter-day Saint members performed proxy baptisms for hundreds of thousands of Holocaust victims. After Jewish organizations protested, the church signed a 1995 agreement to remove victims' names and stop the practice, except for direct ancestors of members. The researcher Helen Radkey then repeatedly documented violations across two decades. Anne Frank's name was submitted at least a dozen times, and the ordinance performed at least nine times, including in the Santo Domingo Temple in February 2012, which prompted a church condemnation. Simon Wiesenthal's parents were baptized by proxy in early 2012, drawing a formal church apology to the family. The church revised its database controls in 2010 and threatened discipline for violators. The episode exposes the doctrine underneath. D&C 128:15-18 declares that the dead 'cannot be made perfect' without our ordinances, and that vicarious work is 'essential to our salvation.' It rests on one disputed verse, 1 Corinthians 15:29, against the Bible's teaching that judgment follows death (Hebrews 9:27) and that a fixed gulf separates the dead (Luke 16:26) — a point the Book of Mormon itself makes at Alma 34:32-35.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms.response: The church and Mormonr respond that proxy baptism compels no one. The teaching is that the dead may accept or reject the ordinance. So it is an offering, not a conversion after death. The institution honoured the 1995 agreement. Each documented violation was the act of individual members, acting against explicit policy. And the church responded seriously. It removed names. It built database blocks on Holocaust-victim submissions in 2010. It apologized to families. And it warned that violators face loss of temple privileges, or discipline.
holocaust-proxy-baptisms.rationale: Every load-bearing fact is conceded by the church itself. The practice occurred. The 1995 agreement existed. Violations continued for years. And the church publicly condemned and apologized for specific cases, including Wiesenthal and Frank. The individual-members defense is fair as far as it goes. It also concedes the systemic point. A doctrine that makes ordinances for the dead 'essential to our salvation' generates pressure that policy could not contain for two decades. The deeper evangelistic use is doctrinal. The whole temple-for-the-dead system hangs on 1 Corinthians 15:29. Read it against Hebrews 9:27, Luke 16:26, and even Alma 34. Medium severity.

prop-8-campaign.claim: In 2008 the First Presidency had a letter read from every California pulpit, on 29 June. It urged members to 'do all you can' — their 'means and time' — to pass Proposition 8, which stripped same-sex marriage from California law. Ward and stake structures were turned into a precinct operation: assigned donation targets, phone banks, and door-to-door canvassing. It was coordinated with the Protect Marriage coalition, which the church joined at Catholic Archbishop Niederauer's invitation. Members contributed an estimated $20 million, roughly half the Yes campaign's funds, while Latter-day Saints were about 2% of Californians. The church itself reported in-kind contributions, and was later fined by the California Fair Political Practices Commission for reporting them late. The same playbook had run in Hawaii in 1998, and on California's Proposition 22 in 2000. The church's canonized position reads differently: 'We do not believe it just to mingle religious influence with civil government' (D&C 134:9; cf. Matthew 22:21, John 18:36). For evangelism the point is institutional. A church claiming political neutrality directed member resources into civil law. Within a decade it reversed course culturally, supporting the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.
prop-8-campaign.response: The church's Newsroom and FAIR respond that churches have always had the right, and a duty, to speak on moral questions. Marriage is a moral question, not partisan politics. The church endorsed no candidate and no party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition rather than acting alone — Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews, Muslims. Direct institutional spending was a small, disclosed, in-kind amount. Members donated freely, as private citizens. And D&C 134 also says governments should protect the free exercise of conscience, which the church argues is what it was doing.
prop-8-campaign.rationale: The facts are documented and not denied. The First Presidency letter. The fundraising run through church channels. The dominant member share of campaign funds. The FPPC fine. The church's defense justifies its involvement rather than disputing it, so the substance is graded admitted. Whether religious political advocacy is wrong is a judgment call Christians themselves divide over. So the entry's force is narrower. It lies in the mismatch with the canonized separation language of D&C 134:9. And it lies in the pattern of mobilize, then soften — Proposition 8, the 2015 exclusion policy, the 2019 reversal, then Respect for Marriage — and in what that implies about revelation tracking public pressure. Medium severity.

huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.claim: In 2021 James Huntsman, of the prominent Huntsman family, sued the church for fraud, seeking the return of roughly $5 million in tithing. He cited President Hinckley's assurance in general conference in 2003 about the City Creek mall project: 'tithing funds have not and will not be used to acquire this property.' Against it he set the whistleblower David Nielsen's account that Ensign Peak Advisors, whose portfolio was built from surplus tithing, moved about $1.4 billion toward City Creek. A Ninth Circuit panel revived the claim in 2023. But on 31 January 2025 an 11-0 en banc court ruled for the church. Six judges held that no reasonable juror could find misrepresentation, because Hinckley in the same address said funds would come from 'commercial entities owned by the Church' and from 'earnings of invested reserve funds.' The remaining judges would have barred the suit under the church-autonomy doctrine. The case matters as the highest-profile legal test of the church's tithing representations, adjacent to the SEC's separate $5 million Ensign Peak settlement. D&C 119:3-4 and 2 Corinthians 8:20-21 are the texts at issue.
