huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.response: The church's defense, accepted by the en banc majority, is that Hinckley's full 2003 statement distinguished tithing principal from 'earnings of invested reserve funds' and from commercial-entity money. City Creek was funded from the latter. So there was no misrepresentation, let alone fraud, and Huntsman produced no evidence that tithing principal was spent. The concurring judges added that the First Amendment's church-autonomy doctrine forbids civil courts from adjudicating what a church told members about sacred donations at all.
huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.rationale: After full adversarial testing, the fraud theory failed 11-0 — and for a majority it failed on the merits, not merely on constitutional avoidance. Hinckley's own contemporaneous wording anticipated the earnings-versus-principal distinction. So the residual complaint reduces to whether earnings on invested tithing are morally 'tithing,' which is a semantic and ethical quarrel rather than a demonstrated deception. Honest grading requires calling this answered. The church won this one. The broader transparency concern is real, but it belongs to the SEC and Ensign Peak entry, which stands on its own. Low severity: citing Huntsman as if it proved fraud would damage the evangelist's credibility.

paul-h-dunn-fabrications.claim: Paul H. Dunn, a General Authority and Seventy from 1964 to 1989, and one of the church's most beloved speakers, built talks and bestselling books on war and baseball stories that were fabricated. His best friend did not die in his arms in the Second World War, and he never played for the St Louis Cardinals. Lynn Packer's investigation, published by the Arizona Republic in February 1991, documented the fabrications. Dunn initially defended them as necessary 'to illustrate his theological and moral points.' Church leaders had known years earlier; Packer's reporting was suppressed while Dunn was quietly given emeritus status in 1989 'for reasons of age and health.' In October 1991 Dunn published a confession in the Church News: 'I have not always been accurate in my public talks and writings,' acknowledging that he had been censured by the First Presidency and the Twelve. The case is a documented instance of faith-promoting fabrication at the church's highest teaching level, and of the institution managing the image rather than the truth until forced. 2 Nephi 9:34, Ephesians 4:25, Proverbs 12:22 and Romans 3:7-8 are the texts at issue.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications.response: FAIR responds that Dunn's dishonesty was personal failure, not church policy. The institution investigated, censured him, moved him to emeritus status, and required a public apology, which is evidence of accountability rather than cover-up. Latter-day Saints do not claim their leaders are infallible or sinless. One man's embellished sermons say nothing about whether the Restoration is true, any more than a dishonest pastor disproves Protestantism. His apology, and the church's acceptance of it, model repentance.
paul-h-dunn-fabrications.rationale: Dunn's own published confession and admitted censure settle the facts, and the church-owned Deseret News reported both. The apologetic point that one leader's sins do not falsify the religion is correct, which is why severity is low. This entry's value is as pattern evidence, not proof. What it legitimately illustrates is the ecology of 'faith-promoting' testimony — emotionally powerful stories generating a spiritual witness in hearers who took that feeling as confirmation — and the institution's preference for quiet management, 'for age and health,' over candour until journalism forced the issue. Use it to open the epistemology conversation, not as a standalone disproof.

hofmann-forgeries-church-response.claim: From 1980 to 1985 the forger Mark Hofmann sold or donated to the church a stream of fake founding-era documents. The 'Anthon transcript' in 1980. The Joseph Smith III blessing in 1981, quietly traded to the RLDS church. And the 'salamander letter' in 1984, in which 'Martin Harris' describes a white salamander, not an angel, guarding the plates; Steve Christensen bought it for $40,000 and donated it to the church. Senior leaders, including Gordon B. Hinckley, met Hofmann repeatedly and acquired sensitive items, some held in the First Presidency vault, and leaders publicly downplayed what the church possessed. No apostle, seer or revelator discerned the fraud. It unravelled only when Hofmann, fearing exposure, murdered Christensen and Kathy Sheets with pipe bombs in October 1985, and the forensic examiner George Throckmorton proved the forgeries. The church's own history-topics essay now recounts the episode. The test is this: leaders sustained as 'seers,' with D&C 46:23-27 promising the church discernment against deception, authenticated by acquisition a set of documents attacking their own founding story, rather than detecting a con man who later said he found deceiving the Brethren easy. 1 John 4:1 and 1 Corinthians 12:10 bear on it.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response.response: FAIR responds that spiritual discernment is not omniscience. God does not shield leaders from ordinary human deception. Scripture shows prophets being deceived in mundane matters. The nation's best document examiners, dealers and historians were fooled too. The church bought documents as any archive acquires material bearing on its history. It published several of them, the salamander letter among them, rather than suppressing them, and it cooperated with prosecutors. Leaders' willingness to engage troubling documents is framed as openness. And Hofmann's success says something about forgery, and nothing about revelation.
hofmann-forgeries-church-response.rationale: The event sequence is conceded in the church's own essay. The meetings. The purchases. The vault. The failure to detect. The murders. Only the significance is disputed. The reply that discernment is not omniscience has force against a cheap gotcha. But it prunes the claims of the office. D&C 46 promises the discerning of spirits precisely 'lest ye be deceived.' And look at what the leaders did. They negotiated for and secured documents that undercut their own founding story. They found a magic-salamander origin plausible enough to buy. That they treated the salamander letter as possibly genuine Martin Harris material is itself telling about the folk-magic world it came from, covered in the seer-stone entry. Medium severity.

burning-in-bosom-epistemology.claim: The entire missionary system rests on Moroni 10:4-5: pray about the Book of Mormon and the Holy Ghost will confirm its truth. It is experienced as a feeling, the 'burning in the bosom' of D&C 9:8-9, which Dallin Oaks describes as 'a feeling of comfort and serenity.' Alma 32:27-28 frames the same experiment. Members are taught that this witness outranks external evidence, and the confirmed feeling then validates the whole chain: book, prophet, priesthood, church. Two problems follow. First, the method cannot discriminate. Muslims, Catholics, evangelicals and Strangites report equivalent confirming experiences for contradictory claims, so at most one set of feelings tracks truth. Second, Scripture commands the opposite order of testing. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 requires rejecting even a sign-working prophet whose doctrine is false. 1 John 4:1 says 'believe not every spirit, but try the spirits.' Isaiah 8:20 says 'to the law and to the testimony.' The Bereans 'searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so' (Acts 17:11). And 'the heart is deceitful above all things' (Jeremiah 17:9). Biblically, doctrine tests experience, never the reverse.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.response: FAIR argues that personal revelation is thoroughly biblical. 'Ask of God,' says James 1:5. Hearts burned on the Emmaus road, in Luke 24:32. Peter's testimony came 'not by flesh and blood,' in Matthew 16:17. The witness is not raw emotion. It is knowledge borne by the Spirit. And D&C 9:8 commands study first, so the feeling confirms the work rather than replacing it. Other faiths having spiritual experiences is to be expected, since God gives light to all people. Such experiences may soften a heart toward God in general, without tying a person to one specific claim. And critics who reduce every spiritual experience to brain chemistry prove too much, since that would undo Christian conversion too.
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.rationale: The apologetic defends the claim that God can speak, and the Christian gladly grants it. It never answers the actual objection. How does a feeling tell true claims from false ones, when religions that contradict each other produce the same feeling? FAIR makes one concession that costs a great deal. It grants that spiritual experiences may not tie a person to one specific claim. That is exactly the use Moroni 10:4 is put to. The missionary program treats the feeling as certifying a whole set of very specific claims. And Deuteronomy 13:1-3 forecloses the move in principle, because even a real supernatural experience must yield to doctrinal testing. This is arguably the keystone entry. Every other case here is waved off by appeal to the testimony this method produces. High severity.

chiasmus-alma-36.claim: This is the strongest literary argument for Book of Mormon antiquity. In 1969 John Welch identified extended chiasmus in the Book of Mormon. Chiasmus is inverted parallelism: A-B-C-C'-B'-A'. Alma 36 is the showpiece — a full-chapter structure pivoting on 'born of God,' argued to reflect an ancient Hebrew form Joseph Smith could not have known. The critical response is led by Earl Wunderli, in 'Critique of Alma 36 as an Extended Chiasm,' published in Dialogue in 2005. He shows that Welch's outline depends on selective labelling. Some repeated words are counted as structure, while others that break the pattern are not. Text in between is skipped. Loose matches are allowed. By Welch's own fifteen criteria, the chapter scores poorly. Chiasm-like patterns also appear where nobody claims Hebrew antiquity: in the Doctrine and Covenants, and in ordinary nineteenth-century prose. Chiasmus scholarship predated the Book of Mormon, such as John Jebb's 'Sacred Literature' of 1820, though Smith's access to it is undemonstrated. The physicists Boyd and Farrell Edwards countered statistically that Alma 36's chiastic ordering is unlikely by chance, and Wunderli rebutted their choice of elements. Genesis 9:6 and Amos 5:4-6 are biblical examples of the form.
chiasmus-alma-36.response: The Edwardses' statistical analysis estimates a low probability that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into chiastic order by chance. They argue that their method does not depend on Welch's or Wunderli's contestable literary criteria. Apologists add that the structure is thematically apt, with conversion at the centre of an inverted life story. They argue that candidate chiasms in the Doctrine and Covenants are demonstrably weaker. And they note that there is no evidence Joseph Smith encountered Jebb, or any chiasmus scholarship, in rural New York before 1829.
chiasmus-alma-36.rationale: This is a genuine two-sided scholarly exchange in peer venues. Wunderli's critique of the selection lands. But the Edwardses' statistical reply is a serious counter, and it survives his rebuttal at least in part. Grading it contested, rather than dismissed, is both accurate and credibility-building. The deeper point for the evangelist is this. Even granting a deliberate chiasm in Alma 36, the step to antiquity fails on its own. A writer soaked in King James parallelism could produce inverted structure. Chiasmus appears in modern texts. And a shape on the page cannot outweigh the anachronism, DNA and textual evidence elsewhere in this app. Low severity: concede the phenomenon, contest the inference.

nahom-nhm-altars.claim: This is the apologists' flagship archaeological evidence. 1 Nephi 16:34 says Ishmael was buried 'in the place which was called Nahom' — a name the party did not coin — after which the group turned 'nearly eastward' (1 Nephi 17:1). Three limestone altars excavated from the Bar'an temple near Marib, in Yemen, from 1988 onward, carry dedications by a donor of the NHM, or Nihm, tribe. They date to roughly the seventh or sixth century BC, which is Lehi's era, and the Nihm tribal region lies near where the frankincense trail bends east toward the coast. Warren Aston and Scripture Central present this as a precise external hit. Critics respond that the inscriptions are three consonants naming a tribe, not a place called Nahom; that the NHM root is common across Semitic names; that the eastward turn matches incense-trail geography generally; and that a form of the name, 'Nehhm,' appears on European maps from Carsten Niebuhr's expedition, in English by 1792. So the correlation is explainable by common naming plus coincidence. Non-Mormon archaeologists attach no significance to the parallel; Philip Jenkins wrote that 'there's no there there.' Proverbs 18:17 is the principle at stake.
nahom-nhm-altars.response: Aston and Scripture Central argue that NHM is rare as an Arabian toponym, and that the altars independently anchor the tribal name to precisely Lehi's period and region — something unknowable from 1820s New York. They note that no evidence connects Joseph Smith to Niebuhr's maps. And they stress convergence: a burial place bearing a mourning-related Semitic root, since NHM connotes consolation and mourning; positioned exactly where the text turns the party east; and terminating at plausible 'Bountiful' candidates on the Omani coast. That chain of hits, they argue, multiplies well beyond coincidence.
nahom-nhm-altars.rationale: Honesty requires ranking this as the best single apologetic datum. It is a real inscriptional correlate, correctly dated and plausibly located. It is also far weaker than presented. A tribal name of three consonants. A root common in Semitic naming. A turn that follows the trade route everyone took. And a name available on published maps decades before 1829 — with academic archaeology outside Mormonism seeing nothing evidentiary in it. Both sides field serious arguments from real data, which is the definition of contested. For the evangelist: grant Nahom its full weight, then note that one consonant cluster in Arabia cannot offset the total absence of Nephite evidence in the New World, where the story's thousand years unfold.

succession-crisis.claim: When Joseph Smith was killed in June 1844, he left no unambiguous succession plan, and the movement fractured among rival claimants. There was his counselor Sidney Rigdon; the Quorum of the Twelve under Brigham Young; and James Strang, who produced a letter of appointment dated June 1844, now at Yale's Beinecke Library and catalogued as 'attributed.' Strang then unearthed his own metal plates at Voree, Wisconsin, in 1845, before four witnesses, and there is no direct contemporaneous evidence that his witnesses ever recanted — a fact that complicates appeals to the Book of Mormon witnesses. Strikingly, the people who knew Joseph best did not go west. His widow Emma stayed in Nauvoo, married the non-Mormon Lewis Bidamon, and in her 1879 'Last Testimony' in the Saints' Herald of 1 October denied to her death that Joseph practised polygamy: 'He had no other wife but me.' His mother Lucy and brother William never gathered to Utah. His son Joseph Smith III became prophet of the rival RLDS church at Amboy, Illinois, in 1860. And none of the Three Witnesses went west in 1847. All were excommunicated by 1838. Oliver Cowdery was rebaptized in 1848 but died before reaching Utah. Martin Harris came only in 1870. David Whitmer never returned. D&C 28:2-7, D&C 43:3-4 and 3 Nephi 11:29 bear on it, as do 1 Corinthians 14:33, Matthew 7:15-20 and Deuteronomy 18:21-22.
succession-crisis.response: Apologists answer that succession did not depend on family. Joseph conferred the keys of the kingdom on the Quorum of the Twelve before his death, and the great majority of Nauvoo Saints sustained the Twelve over Rigdon on 8 August 1844. Strang's letter of appointment is judged a forgery on handwriting and postal grounds, and apologists contend that several Voree witnesses later distanced themselves from Strang. As for Emma, FAIR argues that her denials are contradicted by overwhelming documentary evidence, including sealing records naming her participation in 1843. They are explained by her desire to protect her sons, her opposition to polygamy, her property disputes with Brigham Young, and her loyalty to the movement her son led. Family proximity, they note, is not the biblical test of truth.
succession-crisis.rationale: Every constituent fact is conceded on all sides. No written succession plan was ever produced. Emma and the Smith family rejected Brigham Young. Joseph Smith III led the rival RLDS church. And Emma denied polygamy until death. What remains contested is the meaning. The keys-to-the-Twelve argument has genuine historical support, and the majority of Nauvoo Saints did follow the Twelve, so this cannot be graded unrefuted. But the defense carries a heavy cost the apologists rarely name. It requires asserting that the prophet's own widow lied publicly and consistently for thirty-five years, while treating friendly witnesses as unimpeachable. And the standard dismissal of Strang's plates, and of witnesses who never fully recanted, applies with uncomfortable symmetry to the Book of Mormon's own witness apparatus.

second-anointing.claim: Beyond the endowment sits a higher ordinance most Latter-day Saints have never heard of: the second anointing, in which a couple's 'calling and election is made sure' and exaltation is sealed upon them. Compare D&C 131:5, 'the more sure word of prophecy,' and D&C 132:49. It has been administered since 28 September 1843, by invitation of the First Presidency only. David John Buerger's landmark study in Dialogue in 1983 documents thousands performed in the nineteenth century, then a sharp curtailment and near-total concealment in the twentieth; the church stopped publishing statistics by the 1930s. Even the apologetic site Mormonr confirms that the ordinance exists, is invitation-only, 'isn't generally taught in Church meetings or in Church publications,' and that teachers are instructed not to discuss it or answer questions about it. It came to broad public light in 2012, when Tom Phillips, a former stake president who received the rite from the apostle M. Russell Ballard, published a detailed firsthand account and told his story on Mormon Stories. Scripture offers assurance of salvation freely to every believer — 1 John 5:13, Romans 8:16, 2 Peter 1:10, Ephesians 2:8-9 — not as a secret rite reserved for elites.
second-anointing.response: Defenders do not deny that the ordinance exists. They defend its privacy. Mormonr frames the second anointing as sacred rather than secret, treated with the same reticence as other temple matters, and not a conspiracy. They note biblical precedent for anointing individuals, since priests and kings were anointed, and Jesus spoke of mysteries given to some and not to others. They stress that the ordinance is conditional rather than an unconditional guarantee of exaltation, so it does not bypass the need for enduring faithfulness. The rarity, they argue, reflects prudence about a blessing that could be misunderstood. And ordinary members lose nothing, since the same blessings are held out to all the faithful, and ordinances not received in this life may be received hereafter. Silence protects sacredness, not a hierarchy of salvation.
second-anointing.rationale: This is graded admitted because the apologetic side itself confirms every factual element. The ordinance exists. It is administered by invitation of the church's highest leadership. It is absent from public teaching. And members are explicitly instructed not to discuss it. The only dispute is characterization — 'sacred' against 'secret' — and whether a conditional sealing differs meaningfully from a guaranteed one. The evangelistic force is untouched by that framing. A two-tier system, in which an inner circle receives a hidden assurance ordinary members do not know exists, stands in stark contrast to the New Testament. There, assurance is proclaimed openly and offered to all believers on the basis of faith in Christ, and 2 Peter 1:10 addresses every reader of a public epistle, not the initiates of a private rite.

jst-whole-bible.claim: From June 1830 to July 1833, Joseph Smith produced an 'inspired revision' of the entire Bible. He altered roughly 3,400 verses, with no manuscript support. And he declared it done: 'We this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' (History of the Church, 2 July 1833). Revelations had commanded that the work be finished (D&C 73:3-4) and published (D&C 124:89). Yet the church has never adopted it. Its official Bible remains the King James Version, with selected readings relegated to footnotes and an appendix. The rival RLDS church, now Community of Christ, published the full text as the Inspired Version in 1867. It held the manuscripts for 150 years. The church bought them in March 2024, with the marked Bible and the Kirtland Temple, in a deal worth $192.5 million. Stranger still, BYU's own scholars concede that the 1830 Book of Mormon was used as a source for some revisions to Isaiah. Yet many Book of Mormon variants were never carried into the revision, and some were changed yet again. So Joseph revised verses that his own earlier scripture quotes in their King James form. 1 Nephi 13:28, D&C 45:60-61 and Articles of Faith 1:8 bear on it, as do Deuteronomy 4:2, Proverbs 30:5-6, Isaiah 40:8 and 1 Peter 1:24-25.
jst-whole-bible.response: FAIR and BYU scholars respond that the July 1833 'finished' statement marked the end of a first pass, not a canon-ready text. Joseph continued revising until his death in 1844. He never prepared a final publication manuscript. And the command to publish, at D&C 124:89, went unfulfilled amid poverty and persecution. So the church inherited an unfinished working draft, not a completed Bible. They add that the revision was never meant as a uniform restoration of original text. It blends textual restoration, prophetic commentary, harmonization and modernization. That explains the divergences from Book of Mormon readings without contradiction. And far from suppressing it, the church put hundreds of its readings into the footnotes and appendix of its 1979 King James edition. The 2024 acquisition reflects reverence for the work, not embarrassment about it.
jst-whole-bible.rationale: The core facts are undisputed. The revision was commanded, pronounced finished in Joseph's own record in 1833, commanded to be published in 1841, never canonized by the church, and published instead by the rival denomination that rejected Brigham Young. The apologetic reply — that it was actually unfinished and multi-genre — is a genuine scholarly position, since Joseph did keep tinkering. That keeps this contested rather than unrefuted. But the defense sits awkwardly with the primary sources. It must read 'we this day finished the translating of the Scriptures' as not meaning finished, and it concedes that the revelation commanding publication was never obeyed. And the category problem remains on any reading. A prophet corrected the Bible by revelation, and the church claiming his mantle still hands members the uncorrected King James.

lectures-on-faith-decanonized.claim: In August 1835 a general assembly of the church voted to canonize the seven Lectures on Faith as the 'Doctrine' half of the Doctrine and Covenants. They are why the book is called Doctrine and Covenants, and they were printed as scripture for 86 years. In 1921 a committee removed them, with no revelation and no vote of common consent. The explanation was that they 'were never presented to nor accepted by the Church as being otherwise than theological lectures' — which contradicts the 1835 assembly minutes accepting the whole volume. The doctrinal driver is plain. Lecture 5 teaches that the Father is 'a personage of spirit,' which is irreconcilable with the later doctrine of D&C 130:22 that the Father has a body of flesh and bones. When the doctrine of God changed, the canon was edited to match. That is a de-canonization, in a church that claims its canon grows only by revelation. Jude 3, Isaiah 40:8 and Malachi 3:6 are the texts at issue.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized.response: FAIR, and Joseph Fielding Smith, who was a member of the 1921 committee, argue that the Lectures were lessons rather than revelations. They were never claimed as the word of the Lord. They were incomplete on the Godhead. And they were removed to avoid confusion with actual revelations. On this view, 1921 was housecleaning rather than de-canonization.
lectures-on-faith-decanonized.rationale: The response concedes the key facts. The 1835 assembly voted to accept the entire book, lectures included, as 'the doctrine and covenants of their faith.' The claim that they were never accepted as more than lessons is contradicted by the 1835 record itself. And 'incomplete on the Godhead' is a euphemism: Lecture 5's spirit-Father theology was superseded, and the canon was trimmed to match. This pairs powerfully with D&C 132 remaining in the canon while being disavowed. The canon is edited by administrative decision, not by revelation. It is conversationally clean, and comes down to one question. What revelation removed them? There is none.

independence-temple-lot-ownership.claim: D&C 57, from 1831, designated Independence, Missouri as the 'center place' of Zion and the spot for the temple. D&C 84:3-5, from 1832, said the temple would be reared there, and D&C 97:19 speaks of it too. Not only was no temple ever built. The church does not even own the dedicated spot today. The actual dedication site belongs to the Church of Christ (Temple Lot), a Hedrickite body of roughly 7,000 members worldwide, which rejects Brigham Young, the endowment, and most Latter-day Saint distinctives. It kept the lot through the Temple Lot litigation of the 1890s, and maintains a modest meetinghouse there. The 17-million-member church whose canon prophesies that temple owns the visitors' center next door. Deuteronomy 18:22 is the test applied. Lead with the ownership irony, not with the 'this generation' dating argument. The dating case belongs with Joseph Smith's failed prophecies, and should not be double-counted here.
independence-temple-lot-ownership.response: The church teaches that the Independence temple will still be built, in the Lord's timing. D&C 124:49 provides that when enemies prevent a commanded work, God no longer requires it of that generation. The church's own question-and-answer page affirms continued belief in a future temple in Zion, and notes cordial relations with the Temple Lot church.
independence-temple-lot-ownership.rationale: The D&C 124:49 escape clause cannot explain the present tense. Nothing prevents the church from building in Jackson County today, except that it does not own the prophesied spot, and the owners will not sell. They have refused offers for over a century. A 194-year-old 'center place' prophecy whose ground is held by a tiny rival restorationist church is vivid, verifiable in five minutes, and hard to spin. It is graded on the ownership core, which is undisputed by all parties, including the church's own materials.

zions-camp-dc105-reversal.claim: In February 1834, D&C 103 promised the redemption of Zion — Jackson County — 'by power,' with the Lord's presence going before the armed expedition. 'The redemption of Zion must needs come by power… I will fight your battles,' and at 103:15-20 his angels would go up before them. Zion's Camp marched roughly 900 miles. Cholera killed about a dozen members. Missouri's governor declined to help. No land was recovered. In June 1834, D&C 105:9-13 called the whole thing off. The Saints must 'wait for a little season for the redemption of Zion,' with the failure attributed to the members' transgressions. Both the promise and its retraction sit in the canon today, alongside D&C 101:17-18. And 192 years later the 'little season' continues, since Jackson County was never redeemed. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and Ezekiel 13:6-7 are the tests applied. Coordinate this with the general failed-prophecies entry, so the D&C 84 temple prophecy is not counted twice.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal.response: Apologists read D&C 103 as conditional. D&C 105 itself explains that the Saints failed to consecrate and were unprepared, so the Lord deferred rather than broke his promise. Zion's Camp is reframed as a refining trial. Many future apostles and seventies were chosen from among its veterans, so the expedition succeeded at its real purpose.
zions-camp-dc105-reversal.rationale: The conditionality was announced after the failure, not before it. D&C 103 reads as an unconditional promise with divine military backing — 'mine angels shall go up before you' — and D&C 105 retrofits conditions once the expedition collapsed. The 'refining trial' reading concedes that the stated objective failed. The unique value here is pedagogical. Unlike disputed prophecy cases, the believer's own canon contains both the promise and the walk-back, so no external source is needed. A 'little season' entering its third century speaks for itself.

one-mighty-and-strong.claim: D&C 85:7-8 promises that God will send 'one mighty and strong, holding the scepter of power in his hand,' to 'set in order the house of God.' The verse is canonized and unfulfilled. So it has bred a steady stream of claimants. A Dialogue survey documents roughly eighteen main ones. By 1905 at least eight had already declared themselves. That forced a First Presidency statement, in the Deseret News in November 1905. It reinterpreted the verse as being about Edward Partridge and land matters in the 1830s. And it declared self-proclaimed candidates ignorant 'of God and the order of the Church.' Founders of fundamentalist sects have claimed the title, and so have violent figures, including the LeBaron clan. A vague canonized prophecy, plus prophetic authority, is a schism engine. And the institutional fix was to reinterpret the scripture by press release. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 and Matthew 24:24 are the tests applied.
one-mighty-and-strong.response: The 1905 First Presidency statement holds that the verse concerned one specific situation in 1832. It was about Bishop Edward Partridge, and land inheritances in Zion. It was likely mooted by Partridge's repentance. And anyone claiming the title today 'manifests great ignorance.' Church materials treat the matter as settled by that statement.
one-mighty-and-strong.rationale: The 1905 statement is itself the interesting fact. For 73 years the verse sat open, and bred claimants. Then the First Presidency closed a canonized prophecy by reinterpreting it in a newspaper. That is a move of authority, not a reading members could have reached from the text. It is not a lead argument. Use it as backing material, on how the canon handles a prophecy that did not come true. It is directly useful when fundamentalist offshoots come up, since nearly every splinter prophet has drafted this verse.

evolution-shifting-statements.claim: The 1909 First Presidency statement 'The Origin of Man' declared Adam 'the first man of all men' and dismissed human evolution as 'theories of men.' The 1925 restatement quietly softened it. Apostles then split publicly for decades. Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie condemned evolution as heresy, incompatible with the Fall. James E. Talmage and B. H. Roberts accepted pre-Adamite life. Today the church's official position is that it has no official position, and BYU teaches evolution as settled science. Meanwhile canonized texts still commit the church to no death before the Fall (2 Nephi 2:22; Alma 12:23-24), to Adam as 'the first flesh upon the earth' (Moses 3:7), and to a 7,000-year temporal history (D&C 77:6-7). Those are claims the church no longer defends, and has never corrected. The question 'who was speaking as a prophet?' has no answer. Genesis 1:26-27 and Romans 5:12 are the texts at issue.
evolution-shifting-statements.response: The church's position is that the 1909 statement affirmed doctrines about humanity's divine origin, not a scientific mechanism. The 1910 and 1925 materials show openness. The church has no official position on evolution itself, and leaves science to science. BYU's board-approved evolution packet reflects that neutrality.
evolution-shifting-statements.rationale: Do not claim that the church banned evolution. It never quite did, and the neutrality framing has real support, in the 1910 Christmas message and in the BYU packet. The strong core is narrower and solid. Apostles taught flatly contradictory positions on a factual question for seventy years, while all claiming prophetic authority. And canonized no-death-before-the-Fall scripture remains uncorrected while functionally abandoned. Use it as a case study in how prophets, seers and revelators resolve empirical questions. They did not. The scientists did, and the church followed. Corroboration, not your lead.

mormon-name-reversal.claim: Between August and October 2018, President Russell M. Nelson declared that using 'Mormon' or 'LDS' for the church 'is a major victory for Satan' and an offense to Jesus. He mandated the full name, triggering renames of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, LDS.org and mormon.org. Yet the church itself had just spent most of a decade, and millions of dollars, on the 'I'm a Mormon' advertising campaign of 2010 to 2018, on the feature film 'Meet the Mormons' in 2014, and on official pages calling 'Mormon' an 'inoffensive nickname.' Gordon B. Hinckley, as prophet, publicly embraced the term — 'Mormon means more good,' in General Conference in October 1990, responding to then-Elder Nelson's plea for the full name earlier that year. Either the nickname aids Satan, which indicts the prophets who ran the campaigns, or it does not, and 'victory for Satan' was rhetorical inflation delivered as prophetic correction. Nelson said the change was 'not a name change… it is a correction' commanded by the Lord. D&C 115:4 and 3 Nephi 27:7-8 are cited for it; Acts 11:26 and 1 Corinthians 1:12-13 are cited against.
mormon-name-reversal.response: Nelson taught that the Lord named the church in D&C 115:4, and that restoring the full name honours Christ. Prior nickname campaigns were well-intentioned accommodations to public awareness. And prophets can receive updated direction, line upon line, without prior leaders being condemned.
mormon-name-reversal.rationale: This is a soft case doctrinally, but it is documented end to end from church sources, and it is constantly live in conversation — 'why can't we say Mormon anymore?' Its value is as an accessible, low-stakes specimen of the pattern the bigger cases show. A prophet framed a reversal of his predecessors' publicly taught position as timeless divine will, with 'Satan' attached to what the church itself did until that year. Use it as a gentle door-opener, not a centerpiece.

lost-116-pages.claim: Martin Harris lost the first 116 manuscript pages, the Book of Lehi, in the summer of 1828. Joseph Smith did not retranslate them. Instead a revelation, now D&C 10, explained that wicked men had altered the lost pages, and would publish the altered version to discredit him. It directed him to translate the 'small plates of Nephi' instead — a second record, covering the same period, which Mormon says he included 'for a wise purpose… I know not' (Words of Mormon 1:3-7). Critics argue this is the signature of a human author who cannot reproduce a lost draft word for word. It is a test that would have been trivially passable for a text delivered word for word on a seer stone. 1 Nephi 9:2-6 and 19:1-6 are the internal references.
lost-116-pages.response: Three replies. First, the stated rationale is counter-forgery, not evasion. If enemies held the only other copy, a fresh translation differing in any wording — as dictated translation inevitably would — could be paraded as proof of fabrication. Declining the trap is the rational move. Second, the 'convenient replacement' framing ignores that the small plates are foreshadowed inside the text, at 1 Nephi 9 and 19, as a second record made by Nephi. Mormon's explicit 'I know not' why he included them reads as an ancient editor recording a prompting he did not understand, which is a strange thing for a fabricator to invent. Third, believers read this as divine foreknowledge providing for a foreseen failure, and the episode is the origin of a permanent lesson about Joseph's fallibility in D&C 3.
lost-116-pages.rationale: This turns entirely on prior probability, since both sides agree on every fact. The apologetic reading is internally coherent, and the point about wording variation is genuinely correct about translation. But the naturalistic reading is the more economical explanation, with one specific edge. The seer-stone method as now officially described, with fixed English words appearing on the stone, is a tight-control model. Under it, a retranslation should have matched, which neutralizes the wording objection. The apologetic defense and the church's own translation essay are in mild tension. Nothing here is falsifiable either way.

witnesses-character-and-vision.claim: The Eleven Witnesses were all Smith family, Whitmer family, or Martin Harris. There were no disinterested observers, and they shared a documented folk-magic worldview that included 'second sight.' Harris and Whitmer later described the experience in visionary terms; Harris spoke of 'the eyes of faith' and 'spiritual eyes,' and Stephen Burnett's 1838 letter reports Harris saying the witnesses saw the plates only in vision. All Three left or were excommunicated by 1838. Whitmer's 1887 pamphlet declared that God told him by voice to leave the church — the same evidentiary channel he claimed for the plates. Harris subsequently endorsed the Shaker 'Sacred Roll,' which also carried multi-witness testimony of angelic visitation. And no witness ever claimed to view the uncovered plates in a mundane, non-visionary setting. Deuteronomy 19:15 and 2 Corinthians 13:1 set the standard for witnesses; Ether 5:2-4 and 2 Nephi 27:12-13 promise them.
witnesses-character-and-vision.response: Four replies, and the first is the strongest fact on this side. Not one of the eleven ever recanted. That includes Cowdery, Harris and Whitmer after bitter excommunications, when recantation would have cost nothing and gained vindication. Whitmer, who never returned, reaffirmed the testimony to hostile interviewers for 50 years, and had it carved on his gravestone. Second, the Eight Witnesses' experience was explicitly ordinary and daylit. They 'hefted' and 'handled' the plates with no angel involved — a different evidentiary category, untouched by the 'spiritual eyes' argument. Third, Richard Lloyd Anderson, in Investigating the Book of Mormon Witnesses (1981), shows that 'spiritual eyes' in nineteenth-century usage frequently means an objectively real perception granted by the Spirit, as at 2 Kings 6:17; most such quotations are late, secondhand, or hostile paraphrases. Fourth, the Whitmer-left point cuts the other way. A man who denounced Smith as fallen and never came back is precisely the witness whose sustained affirmation is hardest to explain as social pressure.
witnesses-character-and-vision.rationale: This is genuinely two-sided, and the strongest surviving apologetic position in this list. The non-recantation record is real and not easily dismissed, especially Whitmer. Against that, the witnesses are not independent; they were kin and business partners in a single religious enterprise. Their epistemology admitted visionary perception as 'seeing.' And Harris's willingness to extend comparable endorsement to the Shaker book materially devalues his testimony as a discriminating instrument. Be suspicious of any source that presents this one as settled. The criticism is weaker than critics claim, and the defense stronger. But sincerity of witnesses establishes sincerity, not the objective content of what was witnessed.

gold-plates-never-examined.claim: The plates were reportedly kept covered or hidden. They were shown only to insiders Smith chose — family, financial backers, early believers. The Three Witnesses saw them in vision. The Eight saw them in a private setting. Then they were returned to the angel. So no scholar, no scientist and no neutral third party ever inspected them. Weight estimates from those who hefted the covered object cluster around 40 to 60 pounds. A solid gold block of the described size would weigh well over 100 to 200 pounds. The object at the centre of the founding claim is gone for good, and cannot be checked.
gold-plates-never-examined.response: Apologists argue that the reported weight fits a real ancient artifact. Tumbaga is a copper-gold alloy, gilded at the surface, and it was used in Mesoamerica. Plates of that size in tumbaga would weigh roughly 53 to 58 pounds, and would look like gold. A forger guessing at 'gold plates' would be unlikely to land on that. The return to the angel is explained from scripture: the record was not meant to convince by proof, and Ether 5 says witnesses were appointed instead. And Richard Lloyd Anderson's work shows those witnesses stayed constant for life.
gold-plates-never-examined.rationale: The core fact is conceded by all sides. No independent examination ever happened, and none is possible now. The tumbaga answer makes the reported weight add up. It cannot stand in for the missing object. What is left in dispute is only how much weight the insider witnesses can carry instead.

kinderhook-plates.claim: In 1843 three men made six bell-shaped brass plates, cut fake 'ancient' characters into them, and planted them in an Illinois mound. They then delivered them to Joseph Smith, to test whether he would translate them. Smith's clerk William Clayton recorded that Smith said the plates held 'the history of the person with whom they were found… a descendant of Ham through the loins of Pharaoh.' That statement entered the official History of the Church in the first person: 'I have translated a portion of them.' Wilbur Fugate confessed the hoax in 1879. Testing in 1980 destroyed part of a plate and confirmed a nineteenth-century brass fake.
kinderhook-plates.response: This is the church's own current published position. Joseph Smith never claimed a revealed translation, and never produced a translated text. Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee, in 'President Joseph Has Translated a Portion' (2011), identify a specific character match against Smith's Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. That makes the identification a secular, comparative exercise. Smith took the matter no further, and dropped the subject. That is the opposite of a con artist walking into a baited trap. The first-person wording is a known artifact of the History of the Church, which turned clerks' journals into Smith's voice. And the church published the forgery finding itself, in the Ensign in 1981.
kinderhook-plates.rationale: The Bradley and Ashurst-McGee reconstruction is decisive, and it is good scholarship rather than spin. The 'descendant of Ham' content traces to a character match against Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar. So it was a plain comparative identification, not a revealed one. And the church disclosed the forgery finding itself. The residue is narrower than critics present. The identification was still wrong, since the characters mean nothing. That reflects on the reliability of the Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar, which connects straight to the Book of Abraham entry, where the same document is the problem. Treat Kinderhook as answered on its own terms, and as backing for the Book of Abraham case.

source-parallels-voth-late-war.claim: Two books from the 1800s are offered as sources. First, Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews, of 1823 and 1825. It argued that American Indians came from the lost tribes, and it was printed in the town where Oliver Cowdery's family lived. B. H. Roberts, a General Authority, privately compiled a 291-page study of it. He listed about 26 structural likenesses: a divided people, a buried ancient record, the Urim and Thummim, Egyptian writing. It was printed after his death, in 1985. Second, a 2013 computer study compared over 100,000 books printed before 1830. It found a strong word-string match with The Late War, by Gilbert Hunt, from 1816 — a school book about the War of 1812, written on purpose in King James style. Shared items include 'curious workmanship' and the shape of the battle scenes. Critics offer both as evidence that the Book of Mormon came out of its own time and place. Alma 46:12-13, 3 Nephi 24-25 and the shape of Ether are the passages cited, against Ezekiel 37:15-20 and Isaiah 18.
source-parallels-voth-late-war.response: Three replies. Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him for the prosecution misstates what he said. There is also no evidence Joseph Smith saw View of the Hebrews before 1830, and he cited it warmly in 1842 as support — which is how a man behaves who found it later. Second, the likenesses are generic to a whole genre of the 1820s about Hebrew origins for the Indians. The books differ on nearly every point. View of the Hebrews has no Christ, no story and no named people, and the Book of Mormon flatly denies the lost-ten-tribes idea it is built on. Third, on The Late War, 75 of the 'significant' matches come from the boilerplate copyright pages. The rest is mostly the King James register both books set out to imitate. The method detects 'wrote in biblical English.' That is the Texas-sharpshooter fallacy. The sharpest attack on the method came from Ryan Thomas, who does not accept Book of Mormon historicity either.
source-parallels-voth-late-war.rationale: The direct-source claims are among the weakest material critics use. Hunting parallels across a huge body of books is unreliable. The copyright-page problem in the Johnson study is a real defect. And a critic himself rejected direct literary dependence. Roberts is routinely misused. What survives is the modest version, and it is well supported. The Book of Mormon is at home in the religious culture of New England in the 1820s. Hebrew origins for the Indians. Anti-Masonic language. The debates over grace and universal salvation behind Alma 40-42. That shows the ideas were in the air. It does not show copying. This app treats the King James and Isaiah dating entries as the strong textual case, and flags these named-source theories with caveats.

book-of-abraham-papyri.claim: Unlike the gold plates, the source documents for the Book of Abraham exist. Smith bought Egyptian papyri in 1835. He declared one roll 'the writings of Abraham while he was in Egypt,' and published the Book of Abraham in 1842. Fragments were rediscovered in 1966. Egyptologists identified them, definitively in Robert Ritner's complete edition of 2011. They are the Breathing Permit of the priest Hor, and portions of the Book of the Dead. Those are standard Ptolemaic funeral texts, about 1,500 years after Abraham. They contain no reference to Abraham at all. Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar maps single characters from the surviving Hor fragment onto long English paragraphs of the published book. And his printed readings of the three facsimiles do not match what Egyptologists read; the female figures in Facsimile 3 are called male kings. This is the only outside, controlled test of Joseph Smith's ability to translate an ancient document. It fails. Abraham 1:1-3 and Genesis 11-12 are the texts at issue.
book-of-abraham-papyri.response: Two defenses, both endorsed in the church's own essay. The first is the missing-scroll theory, from John Gee and Kerry Muhlestein at BYU. The recovered fragments are a small remnant. Eyewitnesses describe a long roll. Gee calculates about 314 centimetres missing from the Hor roll. And much of the collection is thought to have burned in the Chicago fire of 1871. On that view the Abraham text sat on papyrus we do not have. The second is the catalyst theory. Joseph's study of the papyri 'provided an occasion for meditation, reflection, and revelation,' and God gave a revelation about Abraham 'even if that revelation did not directly correlate to the characters.' Two supports follow. The Kirtland Egyptian Papers may be a later scribal attempt to work backwards from a text already revealed. And apologists cite claimed ancient parallels to content that is not in Genesis: the attempted sacrifice of Abraham, Abraham teaching astronomy, and the name 'Olishem' possibly matching the attested place-name Ulisum. Those appear in traditions outside the Bible that Smith is unlikely to have known.
book-of-abraham-papyri.rationale: This is the strongest outside test in the whole corpus. The source document exists, and Egyptology is a mature science with no Latter-day Saint stake in it. The church has conceded the core fact in an official essay. The two defenses each make sense alone. Together they are telling, because they contradict each other. Either the Abraham text was on a lost papyrus, which makes the translation real and the fragments beside the point. Or the papyri were only a prompt, which makes the lost scroll beside the point. The missing-scroll theory has one problem it has not overcome. Smith's own Egyptian Alphabet and Grammar lines up characters from the surviving fragment against verses of the Book of Abraham. That puts his working source in documents we hold. The catalyst theory cannot be tested. And it dissolves the word 'translation' as the church used it for 130 years, which drains force from the Book of Mormon translation claim too. The proposed parallels, such as Olishem, are of the weak type flagged elsewhere, and cannot offset a direct mismatch in decipherment.

stylometry-wordprint-studies.claim: Two opposed bodies of computer work on authorship exist. On the pro-historicity side, Larsen, Rencher and Layton in BYU Studies in 1980, and Hilton in BYU Studies in 1990. They reported that the Book of Mormon's internal narrators can be told apart, from each other and from Joseph Smith. On the other side, Jockers, Witten and Criddle, in Literary and Linguistic Computing in 2008. They applied a method called nearest-shrunken-centroid, and concluded that the chapters point most strongly to Solomon Spalding and Sidney Rigdon. That would support the Spalding-Rigdon theory of how the book was written.
stylometry-wordprint-studies.response: G. Bruce Schaalje, a BYU statistician, and his colleagues found the decisive flaw. The method is a closed-set classifier. It is obliged by its own maths to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you give it. Joseph Smith's own writings were largely left out of the pool, while Rigdon and Spalding were put in. Schaalje extended the method so that it could return 'author not in the set,' and reran it on the same data. Rigdon and Spalding each scored 0%. The probability of an author outside the set came out at 93%. Separately, the Spalding-Rigdon theory is rejected by nearly all historians of Mormonism, believers and non-believers alike, including Fawn Brodie and Dan Vogel. The documents give Rigdon no traceable contact with Smith before late 1830, after the book was printed.
stylometry-wordprint-studies.rationale: This is lopsided, and worth using as a lesson in method. The critical study is the weaker one. Schaalje's closed-set objection is correct, and mainstream historians reject the Spalding-Rigdon theory on other grounds, so treat that study as answered. But the studies on the other side do not therefore win. Telling several voices apart does not tell an ancient author from one writer making distinct characters. That is a known limit of the method on narrative fiction. And the same 'author not in the set' logic cuts against any positive ancient attribution. Stylometry as now practised cannot settle who wrote the Book of Mormon, in either direction. Discount confident claims from either camp.

jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.claim: Joseph Smith's revision of the Bible, made between 1830 and 1833, expands Genesis 50 with roughly 14 verses. In JST Genesis 50:24-38 the patriarch Joseph prophesies a latter-day 'choice seer' named Joseph, whose father is also named Joseph. That matches Joseph Smith Jr., son of Joseph Smith Sr. The same prophecy appears at 2 Nephi 3:6-18 and 4:1-2, which quote the 'lost' Genesis material. No ancient version contains this passage. Not a Hebrew manuscript. Not the Septuagint. Not a Dead Sea Scroll, the Samaritan Pentateuch, or any targum. The entire known textual tradition of Genesis ends chapter 50 without it.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.response: Latter-day Saint scholarship — Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson, echoed by FAIR — grants that no ancient manuscript contains the passage. It argues that the revision was never claimed to be purely a restoration of lost text. It can be restoration of content, inspired commentary, harmonization, or prophetic expansion adapted to a latter-day audience. On that view, JST Genesis 50 may restore a genuine prophecy preserved on the brass plates. That would be why it also appears in 2 Nephi 3. It would have dropped out of the Hebrew tradition very early. Or it may be revealed content that was never in the biblical text at all. Either way its authority rests on revelation, not on manuscripts.
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.rationale: The textual fact is conceded on all sides. Zero ancient witnesses contain the passage, and the prophecy names the revelator himself. The apologetic response does not rebut the evidence. It reclassifies the revision so that missing manuscript support cannot count against it. That is unfalsifiable rather than a refutation.

angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.claim: Joseph Smith's official manuscript history of 1838 and 1839 names the angel of the gold plates 'Nephi,' not Moroni. It was published that way under his own editorship, in the Times and Seasons of 15 April 1842. The 'Nephi' reading was reprinted in the Millennial Star in 1842, in the first edition of the Pearl of Great Price in 1851, and in Lucy Mack Smith's history of 1853. Smith lived two years after the 1842 printing and published no correction. Later editions silently emended the name to Moroni.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.response: FAIR and church historians argue that the 'Nephi' reading was a scribal or editorial error, introduced when clerks compiled the history in 1838 and 1839. Sources earlier than 1842 already identify the messenger as Moroni — Oliver Cowdery's 1835 letters in the Messenger and Advocate, and D&C 27:5, also from 1835. So 'Moroni' predates 'Nephi' in the record. Joseph Smith did not personally proofread every installment of the serialized history. And the church corrected the name to match the earlier, better-attested identification, rather than covering anything up.
angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.rationale: The publication history is undisputed primary-source fact. 'Nephi' stood in sources from 1842 to 1853, and was later emended. The apologetic point that 1835 sources name Moroni first is also solid, which makes a clerical error genuinely plausible. What remains unexplained is why the error propagated uncorrected through several official publications, during and after Smith's lifetime.

first-vision-multiple-accounts.claim: Joseph Smith left at least four firsthand accounts of his First Vision, and they differ on core details. The 1832 account, in his own hand, describes one personage, 'the Lord.' It gives his age as about 15 or 16. It says he had already concluded that all the churches were wrong before he prayed. And it does not mention a revival. The 1835 account describes one personage followed by another, plus 'many angels.' The canonized 1838 account describes two personages, the Father and the Son, gives his age as 14, and makes an 1820 revival the trigger. The 1842 Wentworth letter describes 'two glorious personages.' The 1832 account was unpublished, and effectively unknown to members until the 1960s.
first-vision-multiple-accounts.response: The church's Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues that the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory, rather than fabrication. The 1832 account emphasizes personal forgiveness, while the 1838 account emphasizes the founding of the church, and retellings that grow in detail are normal for repeated autobiographical narration. Historians such as Milton Backman and James Allen argue that the accounts are complementary. 'The Lord' in 1832 can encompass two personages. And multiple tellings with varying emphases are evidence of an authentic core experience, rather than an evolving invention.
first-vision-multiple-accounts.rationale: The existence and content of the differing accounts is established primary-source fact, which the church itself now publishes. The dispute is whether the differences are harmonizable variation in memory, or evidence of an evolving story. The sharpest of those differences are one personage against two, and a quest for forgiveness against a question about which church is true. Both readings are argued by credentialed historians.

first-vision-revival-dating.claim: The canonized 1838 account ties the First Vision to an 'unusual excitement on the subject of religion' in the Palmyra area in 1820, which added 'great multitudes' to the churches. Wesley Walters examined Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist records, in work published in 1967 and 1969. He found no significant revival or membership surge in the Palmyra area in 1819 or 1820. What he found was a large, well-documented revival in 1824 and 1825 — after Moroni's claimed visit of 1823. That suggests Smith projected the later revival back into the 1820 narrative.
first-vision-revival-dating.response: Milton Backman replied directly, in 'Awakenings in the Burned-over District' in BYU Studies in 1969. He documented Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819 and 1820, and revival activity across the broader Genesee region. He argued that Smith described a regional awakening, not a formal Palmyra revival with recorded membership gains. The Gospel Topics essay adopts that reading. Smith, recalling his teenage years, described general religious excitement in 'the whole district of country.' A Palmyra camp meeting in 1818, and an 1819 Methodist conference at nearby Vienna, fit his description.
first-vision-revival-dating.rationale: Walters' negative finding stands largely unrebutted in the church records. There was no 1820 Palmyra revival producing 'great multitudes' of converts. But Backman's evidence of regional camp-meeting activity in 1819 and 1820 gives the 1838 account a defensible looser reading. The verdict turns on how literally 'great multitudes' joining churches must be taken.

word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.claim: D&C 89, from 1833, counsels against wine, strong drink, tobacco and 'hot drinks,' later defined as coffee and tea. Its own preamble says it is sent 'not by commandment or constraint' (D&C 89:2). For decades observance was uneven. Under Heber J. Grant, abstinence became a fixed requirement for a temple recommend, formalized by 1921. So a person who drinks coffee or wine cannot enter the temple today, and therefore, in Latter-day Saint teaching, cannot receive the ordinances required for exaltation. Critics set this against the New Testament's explicit release from rules about food and drink. Jesus 'declared all foods clean' (Mark 7:18-19). Paul forbids judging believers 'in meat, or in drink,' and calls 'touch not; taste not; handle not' rules of no value (Colossians 2:16-23). He warns that 'commanding to abstain from meats' marks latter-day apostasy (1 Timothy 4:1-5). And he makes dietary practice a matter of conscience (Romans 14:14-17; cf. Matthew 11:19).
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.response: The steelmanned position is this. The Word of Wisdom is not a purity law, claiming that certain substances defile the soul. It is a revealed health code and a covenant standard: the body as a temple of God, from 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. Any covenant community may set such a standard as a condition of its own ordinances. Biblical precedents include the Nazirite vow, Daniel's abstention, and the Rechabites, all of them commended. The shift from counsel to commandment is explained as prophetic implementation by common consent over time, 'adapted to the capacity of the weak' (D&C 89:3). It is an exercise of the same living prophetic authority Latter-day Saints believe governed dietary rules in both Testaments.
word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.rationale: The historical facts are undisputed and conceded in church sources. It was originally 'not by commandment,' and later hardened into a worthiness gate. Whether that contradicts Scripture is contested. The health-code framing is coherent. But Colossians 2:20-23 and 1 Timothy 4:3 target precisely the practice of making abstinence rules a measure of religious standing. And tying rules about drink to the ordinances that are prerequisites for exaltation presses hard against that text.

temple-garments-practice.claim: Endowed Latter-day Saints covenant to wear the temple garment — a prescribed white underclothing bearing sacred marks. The General Handbook, at 38.5, instructs that it should be worn 'day and night throughout your life,' and never altered. Since 2024 the temple-recommend interview includes a standardized statement on garment wearing, to which members respond, making the practice a recurring worthiness checkpoint. Critics note that the New Testament nowhere prescribes ritual clothing for believers. The claimed biblical analogue is the tzitzit fringes of Numbers 15:38-39 and Deuteronomy 22:12, which were a visible outer sign commanded specifically to Israel under the Mosaic law. And Colossians 2:16-23 warns against measuring Christian standing by outward observance, as do Matthew 23:5 and 1 Samuel 16:7.
temple-garments-practice.response: The church presents the garment as a private, personal reminder of covenants made in the temple. It is offered as analogous to the nun's habit, the priest's cassock, the Jewish prayer shawl, or the Muslim skullcap — 'part of a rich tapestry of human devotion to God.' The church notes that the tzitzit's own stated purpose is the same as the garment's: 'that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD' (Numbers 15:39). Wearing it is framed as keeping a freely made covenant, not as a claim that clothing saves. And the recommend statement is read as covenant accountability rather than legalism.
temple-garments-practice.rationale: The practice, and its enforcement through the interview, are documented from the church's own handbook. Whether it conflicts with Scripture is a normative dispute. The tzitzit parallel is real in function, since both are a sign for remembering. But it belongs to the Mosaic covenant, which Christians hold to be fulfilled. And the Bible neither commands nor forbids such a practice for the church, so the criticism rests on inference rather than on direct contradiction. Treat the practice itself with respect; the question worth asking is about the checkpoint, not the cloth.
